## Tool: custom_tool_call_output

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 9.8 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"f7df49","wall_time_seconds":1.263865,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":15109,"output":"\\r\\nFILE C:\\\\Users\\\\Joshu\\\\dev\\\\ai-os\\\\skills\\\\codex\\\\skill-creator\\\\SKILL.md\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: skill-creator\\r\\ndescription: Guide for creating effective skills. This skill should be used when users want to create a new skill (or update an existing skill) that extends Codex\'s capabilities with specialized knowledge, workflows, or tool integrations.\\r\\nmetadata:\\r\\n  short-description: Create or update a skill\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Skill Creator\\r\\n\\r\\nThis skill provides guidance for creating effective skills.\\r\\n\\r\\n## About Skills\\r\\n\\r\\nSkills are modular, self-contained folders that extend Codex\'s capabilities by providing\\r\\nspecialized knowledge, workflows, and tools. Think of them as \\"onboarding guides\\" for specific\\r\\ndomains or tasks—they transform Codex from a general-purpose agent into a specialized agent\\r\\nequipped with procedural knowledge that no model can fully possess.\\r\\n\\r\\n### What Skills Provide\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Specialized workflows - Multi-step procedures for specific domains\\r\\n2. Tool integrations - Instructions for working with specific file formats or APIs\\r\\n3. Domain expertise - Company-specific knowledge, schemas, business logic\\r\\n4. Bundled resources - Scripts, references, and assets for complex and repetitive tasks\\r\\n\\r\\n## Core Principles\\r\\n\\r\\n### Concise is Key\\r\\n\\r\\nThe context window is a public good. Skills share the context window with everything else Codex needs: system prompt, conversation history, other Skills\' metadata, and the actual user request.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Default assumption: Codex is already very smart.** Only add context Codex doesn\'t already have. Challenge each piece of information: \\"Does Codex really need this explanation?\\" and \\"Does this paragraph justify its token cost?\\"\\r\\n\\r\\nPrefer concise examples over verbose explanations.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Set Appropriate Degrees of Freedom\\r\\n\\r\\nMatch the level of specificity to the task\'s fragility and variability:\\r\\n\\r\\n**High freedom (text-based instructions)**: Use when multiple approaches are valid, decisions depend on context, or heuristics guide the approach.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Medium freedom (pseudocode or scripts with parameters)**: Use when a preferred pattern exists, some variation is acceptable, or configuration affects behavior.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Low freedom (specific scripts, few parameters)**: Use when operations are fragile and error-prone, consistency is critical, or a specific sequence must be followed.\\r\\n\\r\\nThink of Codex as exploring a path: a narrow bridge with cliffs needs specific guardrails (low freedom), while an open field allows many routes (high freedom).\\r\\n\\r\\n### Protect Validation Integrity\\r\\n\\r\\nYou may use subagents during iteration to validate whether a skill works on realistic tasks or whether a suspected problem is real. This is most useful when you want an independent pass on the skill\'s behavior, outputs, or failure modes after a revision.  Only do this when it is possible to start new subagents.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen using subagents for validation, treat that as an evaluation surface. The goal is to learn whether the skill generalizes, not whether another agent can reconstruct the answer from leaked context.\\r\\n\\r\\nPrefer raw artifacts such as example prompts, outputs, diffs, logs, or traces. Give the minimum task-local context needed to perform the validation. Avoid passing the intended answer, suspected bug, intended fix, or your prior conclusions unless the validation explicitly requires them.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Anatomy of a Skill\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery skill consists of a required SKILL.md file and optional bundled resources:\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\nskill-name/\\r\\n├── SKILL.md (required)\\r\\n│   ├── YAML frontmatter metadata (required)\\r\\n│   │   ├── name: (required)\\r\\n│   │   └── description: (required)\\r\\n│   └── Markdown instructions (required)\\r\\n├── agents/ (recommended)\\r\\n│   └── openai.yaml - UI metadata for skill lists and chips\\r\\n└── Bundled Resources (optional)\\r\\n    ├── scripts/          - Executable code (Python/Bash/etc.)\\r\\n    ├── references/       - Documentation intended to be loaded into context as needed\\r\\n    └── assets/           - Files used in output (templates, icons, fonts, etc.)\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n#### SKILL.md (required)\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery SKILL.md consists of:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Frontmatter** (YAML): Contains `name` and `description` fields. These are the only fields that Codex reads to determine when the skill gets used, thus it is very important to be clear and comprehensive in describing what the skill is, and when it should be used.\\r\\n- **Body** (Markdown): Instructions and guidance for using the skill. Only loaded AFTER the skill triggers (if at all).\\r\\n\\r\\n#### Agents metadata (recommended)\\r\\n\\r\\n- UI-facing metadata for skill lists and chips\\r\\n- Read references/openai_yaml.md before generating values and follow its descriptions and constraints\\r\\n- Create: human-facing `display_name`, `short_description`, and `default_prompt` by reading the skill\\r\\n- Generate deterministically by passing the values as `--interface key=value` to `scripts/generate_openai_yaml.py` or `scripts/init_skill.py`\\r\\n- On updates: validate `agents/openai.yaml` still matches SKILL.md; regenerate if stale\\r\\n- Only include other optional interface fields (icons, brand color) if explicitly provided\\r\\n- See references/openai_yaml.md for field definitions and examples\\r\\n\\r\\n#### Bundled Resources (optional)\\r\\n\\r\\n##### Scripts (`scripts/`)\\r\\n\\r\\nExecutable code (Python/Bash/etc.) for tasks that require deterministic reliability or are repeatedly rewritten.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **When to include**: When the same code is being rewritten repeatedly or deterministic reliability is needed\\r\\n- **Example**: `scripts/rotate_pdf.py` for PDF rotation tasks\\r\\n- **Benefits**: Token efficient, deterministic, may be executed without loading into context\\r\\n- **Note**: Scripts may still need to be read by Codex for patching or environment-specific adjustments\\r\\n\\r\\n##### References (`references/`)\\r\\n\\r\\nDocumentation and reference material intended to be loaded as needed into context to inform Codex\'s process and thinking.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **When to include**: For documentation that Codex should reference while working\\r\\n- **Examples**: `references/finance.md` for financial schemas, `references/mnda.md` for company NDA template, `references/policies.md` for company policies, `references/api_docs.md` for API specifications\\r\\n- **Use cases**: Database schemas, API documentation, domain knowledge, company policies, detailed workflow guides\\r\\n- **Benefits**: Keeps SKILL.md lean, loaded only when Codex determines it\'s needed\\r\\n- **Best practice**: If files are large (>10k words), include grep search patterns in SKILL.md\\r\\n- **Avoid duplication**: Information should live in either SKILL.md or references files, not both. Prefer references files for detailed information unless it\'s truly core to the skill—this keeps SKILL.md lean while making information discoverable without hogging the context window. Keep only essential procedural instructions and workflow guidance in SKILL.md; move detailed reference material, schemas, and examples to references files.\\r\\n\\r\\n##### Assets (`assets/`)\\r\\n\\r\\nFiles not intended to be loaded into context, but rather used within the output Codex produces.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **When to include**: When the skill needs files that will be used in the final output\\r\\n- **Examples**: `assets/logo.png` for brand assets, `assets/slides.pptx` for PowerPoint templates, `assets/frontend-template/` for HTML/React boilerplate, `assets/font.ttf` for typography\\r\\n- **Use cases**: Templates, images, icons, boilerplate code, fonts, sample documents that get copied or modified\\r\\n- **Benefits**: Separates output resources from documentation, enables Codex to use files without loading them into context\\r\\n\\r\\n#### What to Not Include in a Skill\\r\\n\\r\\nA skill should only contain essential files that directly support its functionality. Do NOT create extraneous documentation or auxiliary files, including:\\r\\n\\r\\n- README.md\\r\\n- INSTALLATION_GUIDE.md\\r\\n- QUICK_REFERENCE.md\\r\\n- CHANGELOG.md\\r\\n- etc.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe skill should only contain the information needed for an AI agent to do the job at hand. It should not contain auxiliary context about the process that went into creating it, setup and testing procedures, user-facing documentation, etc. Creating additional documentation files just adds clutter and confusion.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Progressive Disclosure Design Principle\\r\\n\\r\\nSkills use a three-level loading system to manage context efficiently:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Metadata (name + description)** - Always in context (~100 words)\\r\\n2. **SKILL.md body** - When skill triggers (<5k words)\\r\\n3. **Bundled resources** - As needed by Codex (Unlimited because scripts can be executed without reading into context window)\\r\\n\\r\\n#### Progressive Disclosure Patterns\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep SKILL.md body to the essentials and under 500 lines to minimize context bloat. Split content into separate files when approaching this limit. When splitting out content into other files, it is very important to reference them from SKILL.md and describe clearly when to read them, to ensure the reader of the skill knows they exist and when to use them.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Key principle:** When a skill supports multiple variations, frameworks, or options, keep only the core workflow and selection guidance in SKILL.md. Move variant-specific details (patterns, examples, configuration) into separate reference files.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Pattern 1: High-level guide with references**\\r\\n\\r\\n```markdown\\r\\n# PDF Processing\\r\\n\\r\\n## Quick start\\r\\n\\r\\nExtract text with pdfplumber:\\r\\n[code example]\\r\\n\\r\\n## Advanced features\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Form filling**: See [FORMS.md](FORMS.md) for complete guide\\r\\n- **API reference**: See [REFERENCE.md](REFERENCE.md) for all methods\\r\\n- **Examples**: See [EXAMPLES.md](EXAMPLES.md) for common patterns\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nCodex loads FORMS.md, REFERENCE.md, or EXAMPLES.md only when needed.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Pattern 2: Domain-specific organization**\\r\\n\\r\\nFor Skills with multiple domains, organize content by domain to avoid loading irrelevant context:\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\nbigquery-skill/\\r\\n├── SKILL.md (overview and navigation)\\r\\n└── reference/\\r\\n    ├── finance.md (revenue, billing metrics)\\r\\n    ├── sales.md (opportunities, pipeline)\\r\\n    ├── product.md (API usage, features)\\r\\n    └── marketing.md (campaigns, attribution)\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen a user asks about sales metrics, Codex only reads sales.md.\\r\\n\\r\\nSimilarly, for skills supporting multiple frameworks or variants, organize by variant:\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\ncloud-deploy/\\r\\n├── SKILL.md (workflow + provider selection)\\r\\n└── references/\\r\\n    ├── aws.md (AWS deployment patterns)\\r\\n    ├── gcp.md (GCP deployment patterns)\\r\\n    └── azure.md (Azure deployment patterns)\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen the user chooses AWS, Codex only reads aws.md.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Pattern 3: Conditional details**\\r\\n\\r\\nShow basic content, link to advanced content:\\r\\n\\r\\n```markdown\\r\\n# DOCX Processing\\r\\n\\r\\n## Creating documents\\r\\n\\r\\nUse docx-js for new documents. See [DOCX-JS.md](DOCX-JS.md).\\r\\n\\r\\n## Editing documents\\r\\n\\r\\nFor simple edits, modify the XML directly.\\r\\n\\r\\n**For tracked changes**: See [REDLINING.md](REDLINING.md)\\r\\n**For OOXML details**: See [OOXML.md](OOXML.md)\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nCodex reads REDLINING.md or OOXML.md only when the user needs those features.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Important guidelines:**\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Avoid deeply nested references** - Keep references one level deep from SKILL.md. All reference files should link directly from SKILL.md.\\r\\n- **Structure longer reference files** - For files longer than 100 lines, include a table of contents at the top so Codex can see the full scope when previewing.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Skill Creation Process\\r\\n\\r\\nSkill creation involves these steps:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Understand the skill with concrete examples\\r\\n2. Plan reusable skill contents (scripts, references, assets)\\r\\n3. Initialize the skill (run init_skill.py)\\r\\n4. Edit the skill (implement resources and write SKILL.md)\\r\\n5. Validate the skill (run quick_validate.py)\\r\\n6. Iterate based on real usage and forward-test complex skills.\\r\\n\\r\\nFollow these steps in order, skipping only if there is a clear reason why they are not applicable.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Skill Naming\\r\\n\\r\\n- Use lowercase letters, digits, and hyphens only; normalize user-provided titles to hyphen-case (e.g., \\"Plan Mode\\" -> `plan-mode`).\\r\\n- When generating names, generate a name under 64 characters (letters, digits, hyphens).\\r\\n- Prefer short, verb-led phrases that describe the action.\\r\\n- Namespace by tool when it improves clarity or triggering (e.g., `gh-address-comments`, `linear-address-issue`).\\r\\n- Name the skill folder exactly after the skill name.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Step 1: Understanding the Skill with Concrete Examples\\r\\n\\r\\nSkip this step only when the skill\'s usage patterns are already clearly understood. It remains valuable even when working with an existing skill.\\r\\n\\r\\nTo create an effective skill, clearly understand concrete examples of how the skill will be used. This understanding can come from either direct user examples or generated examples that are validated with user feedback.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor example, when building an image-editor skill, relevant questions include:\\r\\n\\r\\n- \\"What functionality should the image-editor skill support? Editing, rotating, anything else?\\"\\r\\n- \\"Can you give some examples of how this skill would be used?\\"\\r\\n- \\"I can imagine users asking for things like \'Remove the red-eye from this image\' or \'Rotate this image\'. Are there other ways you imagine this skill being used?\\"\\r\\n- \\"What would a user say that should trigger this skill?\\"\\r\\n- \\"Where should I create this skill? If you do not have a preference, I will place it in `$CODEX_HOME/skills` (or `~/.codex/skills` when `CODEX_HOME` is unset) so Codex can discover it automatically.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\nTo avoid overwhelming users, avoid asking too many questions in a single message. Start with the most important questions and follow up as needed for better effectiveness.\\r\\n\\r\\nConclude this step when there is a clear sense of the functionality the skill should support.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Step 2: Planning the Reusable Skill Contents\\r\\n\\r\\nTo turn concrete examples into an effective skill, analyze each example by:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Considering how to execute on the example from scratch\\r\\n2. Identifying what scripts, references, and assets would be helpful when executing these workflows repeatedly\\r\\n\\r\\nExample: When building a `pdf-editor` skill to handle queries like \\"Help me rotate this PDF,\\" the analysis shows:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Rotating a PDF requires re-writing the same code each time\\r\\n2. A `scripts/rotate_pdf.py` script would be helpful to store in the skill\\r\\n\\r\\nExample: When designing a `frontend-webapp-builder` skill for queries like \\"Build me a todo app\\" or \\"Build me a dashboard to track my steps,\\" the analysis shows:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Writing a frontend webapp requires the same boilerplate HTML/React each time\\r\\n2. An `assets/hello-world/` template containing the boilerplate HTML/React project files would be helpful to store in the skill\\r\\n\\r\\nExample: When building a `big-query` skill to handle queries like \\"How many users have logged in today?\\" the analysis shows:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Querying BigQuery requires re-discovering the table schemas and relationships each time\\r\\n2. A `references/schema.md` file documenting the table schemas would be helpful to store in the skill\\r\\n\\r\\nTo establish the skill\'s contents, analyze each concrete example to create a list of the reusable resources to include: scripts, references, and assets.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Step 3: Initializing the Skill\\r\\n\\r\\nAt this point, it is time to actually create the skill.\\r\\n\\r\\nSkip this step only if the skill being developed already exists. In this case, continue to the next step.\\r\\n\\r\\nBefore running `init_skill.py`, ask where the user wants the skill created. If they do not specify a location, default to `$CODEX_HOME/skills`; when `CODEX_HOME` is unset, fall back to `~/.codex/skills` so the skill is auto-discovered.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen creating a new skill from scratch, always run the `init_skill.py` script. The script conveniently generates a new template skill directory that automatically includes everything a skill requires, making the skill creation process much more efficient and reliable.\\r\\n\\r\\nUsage:\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\nscripts/init_skill.py <skill-name> --path <output-directory> [--resources scripts,references,assets] [--examples]\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nExamples:\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\nscripts/init_skill.py my-skill --path \\"${CODEX_HOME:-$HOME/.codex}/skills\\"\\r\\nscripts/init_skill.py my-skill --path \\"${CODEX_HOME:-$HOME/.codex}/skills\\" --resources scripts,references\\r\\nscripts/init_skill.py my-skill --path ~/work/skills --resources scripts --examples\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThe script:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Creates the skill directory at the specified path\\r\\n- Generates a SKILL.md template with proper frontmatter and TODO placeholders\\r\\n- Creates `agents/openai.yaml` using agent-generated `display_name`, `short_description`, and `default_prompt` passed via `--interface key=value`\\r\\n- Optionally creates resource directories based on `--resources`\\r\\n- Optionally adds example files when `--examples` is set\\r\\n\\r\\nAfter initialization, customize the SKILL.md and add resources as needed. If you used `--examples`, replace or delete placeholder files.\\r\\n\\r\\nGenerate `display_name`, `short_description`, and `default_prompt` by reading the skill, then pass them as `--interface key=value` to `init_skill.py` or regenerate with:\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\nscripts/generate_openai_yaml.py <path/to/skill-folder> --interface key=value\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nOnly include other optional interface fields when the user explicitly provides them. For full field descriptions and examples, see references/openai_yaml.md.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Step 4: Edit the Skill\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen editing the (newly-generated or existing) skill, remember that the skill is being created for another instance of Codex to use. Include information that would be beneficial and non-obvious to Codex. Consider what procedural knowledge, domain-specific details, or reusable assets would help another Codex instance execute these tasks more effectively.\\r\\n\\r\\nAfter substantial revisions, or if the skill is particularly tricky, you should use subagents to forward-test the skill on realistic tasks or artifacts. When doing so, pass the artifact under validation rather than your diagnosis of what is wrong, and keep the prompt generic enough that success depends on transferable reasoning rather than hidden ground truth.\\r\\n\\r\\n#### Start with Reusable Skill Contents\\r\\n\\r\\nTo begin implementation, start with the reusable resources identified above: `scripts/`, `references/`, and `assets/` files. Note that this step may require user input. For example, when implementing a `brand-guidelines` skill, the user may need to provide brand assets or templates to store in `assets/`, or documentation to store in `references/`.\\r\\n\\r\\nAdded scripts must be tested by actually running them to ensure there are no bugs and that the output matches what is expected. If there are many similar scripts, only a representative sample needs to be tested to ensure confidence that they all work while balancing time to completion.\\r\\n\\r\\nIf you used `--examples`, delete any placeholder files that are not needed for the skill. Only create resource directories that are actually required.\\r\\n\\r\\n#### Update SKILL.md\\r\\n\\r\\n**Writing Guidelines:** Always use imperative/infinitive form.\\r\\n\\r\\n##### Frontmatter\\r\\n\\r\\nWrite the YAML frontmatter with `name` and `description`:\\r\\n\\r\\n- `name`: The skill name\\r\\n- `description`: This is the primary triggering mechanism for your skill, and helps Codex understand when to use the skill.\\r\\n  - Include both what the Skill does and specific triggers/contexts for when to use it.\\r\\n  - Include all \\"when to use\\" information here - Not in the body. The body is only loaded after triggering, so \\"When to Use This Skill\\" sections in the body are not helpful to Codex.\\r\\n  - Example description for a `docx` skill: \\"Comprehensive document creation, editing, and analysis with support for tracked changes, comments, formatting preservation, and text extraction. Use when Codex needs to work with professional documents (.docx files) for: (1) Creating new documents, (2) Modifying or editing content, (3) Working with tracked changes, (4) Adding comments, or any other document tasks\\"\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not include any other fields in YAML frontmatter.\\r\\n\\r\\n##### Body\\r\\n\\r\\nWrite instructions for using the skill and its bundled resources.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Step 5: Validate the Skill\\r\\n\\r\\nOnce development of the skill is complete, validate the skill folder to catch basic issues early:\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\nscripts/quick_validate.py <path/to/skill-folder>\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThe validation script checks YAML frontmatter format, required fields, and naming rules. If validation fails, fix the reported issues and run the command again.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Step 6: Iterate\\r\\n\\r\\nAfter testing the skill, you may detect the skill is complex enough that it requires forward-testing; or users may request improvements.\\r\\n\\r\\nUser testing often this happens right after using the skill, with fresh context of how the skill performed.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Forward-testing and iteration workflow:**\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Use the skill on real tasks\\r\\n2. Notice struggles or inefficiencies\\r\\n3. Identify how SKILL.md or bundled resources should be updated\\r\\n4. Implement changes and test again\\r\\n5. Forward-test if it is reasonable and appropriate\\r\\n\\r\\n## Forward-testing\\r\\n\\r\\nTo forward-test, launch subagents as a way to stress test the skill with minimal context.\\r\\nSubagents should *not* know that they are being asked to test the skill.  They should be treated as\\r\\nan agent asked to perform a task by the user.  Prompts to subagents should look like:\\r\\n  `Use $skill-x at /path/to/skill-x to solve problem y`\\r\\nNot:\\r\\n  `Review the skill at /path/to/skill-x; pretend a user asks you to...`\\r\\n\\r\\nDecision rule for forward-testing:\\r\\n  - Err on the side of forward-testing\\r\\n  - Ask for approval if you think there\'s a risk that forward-testing would:\\r\\n    * take a long time,\\r\\n    * require additional approvals from the user, or\\r\\n    * modify live production systems\\r\\n\\r\\n  In these cases, show the user your proposed prompt and request (1) a yes/no decision, and\\r\\n  (2) any suggested modifictions.\\r\\n\\r\\nConsiderations when forward-testing:\\r\\n   - use fresh threads for independent passes\\r\\n   - pass the skill, and a request in a similar way the user would.\\r\\n   - pass raw artifacts, not your conclusions\\r\\n   - avoid showing expected answers or intended fixes\\r\\n   - rebuild context from source artifacts after each iteration\\r\\n   - review the subagent\'s output and reasoning and emitted artifacts\\r\\n   - avoid leaving artifacts the agent can find on disk between iterations;\\r\\n     clean up subagents\' artifacts to avoid additional contamination.\\r\\n\\r\\nIf forward-testing only succeeds when subagents see leaked context, tighten the skill or the\\r\\nforward-testing setup before trusting the result.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\nFILE C:\\\\Users\\\\Joshu\\\\dev\\\\ai-os\\\\skills\\\\codex\\\\skill-doctor\\\\SKILL.md\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: skill-doctor\\r\\ndescription: Use when the user wants their agent setup graded from real conversation history, asks which installed skills are actually working, or wants evidence-backed skill edits — scores recent local Claude Code / Codex sessions against efficiency and code-quality rubrics, then drafts skill changes gated by a deterministic aggregator and renders one local shareable report.\\r\\nlicense: MIT\\r\\nmetadata:\\r\\n  argument_hint: \\"[optional: --repo PATH, --days N, or a question about the setup]\\"\\r\\n  version: 1.0.0\\r\\n  build_pattern: \\"Rebuild of warpdotdev/common-skills skill-doctor (MIT): harvest → LLM-judges-with-rubrics → deterministic aggregation gate → self-contained HTML report\\"\\r\\n  distinct_from: \\"skillopt-sleep (nightly automated replay loop with adopt gate; this is one interactive graded pass); write-a-skill (authors a skill from expertise; this improves skills from observed session evidence); self-eval (grades this session\'s own work; this grades a window of past sessions)\\"\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# skill-doctor — grade the agent setup from real sessions\\r\\n\\r\\nThe bundled scripts parse and write files locally and make no model calls. Scoring by this assistant sends the excerpts it reads to the configured model provider as part of the conversation. A fully local assessment requires a locally hosted model. Redaction is best-effort; inspect only the minimum needed excerpts and never claim provider-side processing is local-only.\\r\\n\\r\\nResolve all script, scorer, asset, and reference paths from **this loaded skill directory**, not the repository being graded. Resolve the target repository separately and pass it as `--repo`. Use a fresh directory under the host\'s temporary directory for outputs. On Windows use PowerShell or Python temporary-directory creation; on POSIX `mktemp -d` is an alternative.\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\npython \\"<skill-root>/scripts/collect_sessions.py\\" --repo \\"<repo-root>\\" --out \\"<run-dir>\\"\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nReplace placeholders with resolved absolute paths before execution. The Python scripts attempt POSIX 0700/0600 permissions; those modes do not establish restrictive Windows ACLs. Do not claim Windows permissions were secured without checking them. Do not collect actual history during installation or instruction repair; use `--help` or `--sample` for checks.\\r\\n\\r\\n**1 — Collect.** Scans Claude Code project-history JSONL and Codex rollouts,\\r\\ndiscovers repo skills (`.claude/skills`, `.agents/skills`, `.codex/skills`, plugin\\r\\nlayouts), detects skill usage (`Skill` invocations, slash commands, SKILL.md paths), samples\\r\\nnewest-first, and writes redacted transcripts. Read `<run-dir>/inventory.json`: if\\r\\n`sessions_sampled` is 0, tell the user there is nothing recent to score (suggest\\r\\n`--days 90` or `--repo`) and stop. `skills_found` 0 is fine — the report becomes a\\r\\ncase for creating skills.\\r\\n\\r\\n**2 — Score.** `python \\"<skill-root>/scripts/score_aggregator.py\\" --inventory \\"<run-dir>/inventory.json\\"\\r\\n--emit-template > \\"<run-dir>/session_scores.json\\"`. Read each transcript in\\r\\n`<run-dir>/transcripts/` and judge it against **both** rubrics — `scorers/efficiency.md`\\r\\nand `scorers/code-quality.md`. Fill the template with a **label from the rubric\'s\\r\\ntable** and a 1–3 sentence reason citing transcript specifics. Never invent numeric\\r\\nscores — the aggregator derives them from labels. Use `insufficient_evidence` when\\r\\na transcript shows no judgeable diff. Also write 1–5 `top_findings`: the most\\r\\nimpactful cross-session patterns, concrete and specific.\\r\\n\\r\\n**3 — Draft edits.** Follow `references/skill_edit_governance.md` (the filing bar:\\r\\nwould a competent agent with the current instructions still fail this way?). For\\r\\neach suggestion that clears it, write the full improved SKILL.md to\\r\\n`<run-dir>/proposed/<skill>/SKILL.md`, produce a unified diff using Python `difflib` or an available diff tool, and record\\r\\nit in `<run-dir>/suggestions.json` citing the sampled session id(s) that motivated it.\\r\\nZero suggestions is a valid success — say why per finding. Never modify the user\'s\\r\\nreal skill files in this step.\\r\\n\\r\\n**4 — Aggregate (the gate).** `python \\"<skill-root>/scripts/score_aggregator.py\\" --inventory\\r\\n\\"<run-dir>/inventory.json\\" --scores \\"<run-dir>/session_scores.json\\" --suggestions\\r\\n\\"<run-dir>/suggestions.json\\"`. It validates labels against the rubric tables, refuses\\r\\nscores for unsampled sessions, requires substantive reasons, rejects suggestions\\r\\nthat cite no scored session, computes `overall = 0.5·efficiency +\\r\\n0.35·code_quality + 0.15·skill_coverage`, and writes `report.json`. **Exit 4 is a\\r\\nstop**: fix what it names and re-run; never hand-edit report.json around it.\\r\\n\\r\\n**5 — Render + tell.** `python \\"<skill-root>/scripts/render_report.py\\" --report \\"<run-dir>/report.json\\"`\\r\\n→ one self-contained `report.html` (no JS, no CDN, dark-mode + print-to-PDF). Then\\r\\ntell the user the grade and the top findings in text, link\\r\\nthe actual absolute local path to `report.html` in a Markdown link, and apply the proposed diffs only if already authorized; otherwise ask whether to apply them — apply only within the scope of explicit user authorization.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Hard rules\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **No separate uploads or publication of transcripts.** Minimize excerpts processed by the configured assistant; disclose provider processing and use a local model if the user requires fully local scoring.\\r\\n2. **Labels only, from the rubric tables.** The aggregator owns all arithmetic.\\r\\n3. **Every suggestion traces to a scored session** — or it is dropped. Generic best practice is not evidence.\\r\\n4. **Zero suggestions is a success**, not a failure to report around.\\r\\n5. **Exit 4 from the aggregator is a stop**, not an error to swallow or bypass.\\r\\n6. **Never touch the user\'s real skill files** without user authorization covering those edits; proposed edits live under `<run-dir>/proposed/`.\\r\\n7. **A proposed skill edit uses concise skill-authoring discipline** — trigger phrase in the description, smallest change that expresses the rule, replace over append.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Scripts\\r\\n\\r\\n| Script | Role | Exit codes |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| `scripts/collect_sessions.py` | Harvest Claude Code + Codex sessions, redact secrets, sample, inventory | 0 · 3 bad input |\\r\\n| `scripts/score_aggregator.py` | Validate labels/reasons/suggestions, compute grade, emit report.json | 0 · 2 warnings · 3 bad input · 4 validation failure |\\r\\n| `scripts/render_report.py` | report.json → single self-contained report.html | 0 · 3 bad input |\\r\\n\\r\\nAll support `--help`, `--output json`, and `--sample` (no real history needed).\\r\\n\\r\\n## References and assets\\r\\n\\r\\n- [`scorers/efficiency.md`](scorers/efficiency.md) · [`scorers/code-quality.md`](scorers/code-quality.md) — the two rubrics, preserved verbatim from upstream\\r\\n- [`references/transcript_scoring_canon.md`](references/transcript_scoring_canon.md) — why rubric-anchored LLM judging works and where it fails (7 sources)\\r\\n- [`references/session_mining_privacy.md`](references/session_mining_privacy.md) — local-script handling, provider-processing limits, and redaction patterns (7 sources)\\r\\n- [`references/skill_edit_governance.md`](references/skill_edit_governance.md) — the filing bar for proposing skill edits (7 sources)\\r\\n- [`assets/session_scores.example.json`](assets/session_scores.example.json) · [`assets/suggestions.example.json`](assets/suggestions.example.json) · [`assets/report.example.json`](assets/report.example.json) — the three handoff shapes\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\nFILE C:\\\\Users\\\\Joshu\\\\dev\\\\ai-os\\\\skills\\\\codex\\\\skill-installer\\\\SKILL.md\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: skill-installer\\r\\ndescription: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos).\\r\\nmetadata:\\r\\n  short-description: Install curated skills from openai/skills or other repos\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Skill Installer\\r\\n\\r\\nHelps install skills. By default these are from https://github.com/openai/skills/tree/main/skills/.curated, but users can also provide other locations. Experimental skills live in https://github.com/openai/skills/tree/main/skills/.experimental and can be installed the same way.\\r\\n\\r\\nUse the helper scripts based on the task:\\r\\n- List skills when the user asks what is available, or if the user uses this skill without specifying what to do. Default listing is `.curated`, but you can pass `--path skills/.experimental` when they ask about experimental skills.\\r\\n- Install from the curated list when the user provides a skill name.\\r\\n- Install from another repo when the user provides a GitHub repo/path (including private repos).\\r\\n\\r\\nInstall skills with the helper scripts.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Communication\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen listing skills, output approximately as follows, depending on the context of the user\'s request. If they ask about experimental skills, list from `.experimental` instead of `.curated` and label the source accordingly:\\r\\n\\"\\"\\"\\r\\nSkills from {repo}:\\r\\n1. skill-1\\r\\n2. skill-2 (already installed)\\r\\n3. ...\\r\\nWhich ones would you like installed?\\r\\n\\"\\"\\"\\r\\n\\r\\nAfter installing a skill, tell the user it will be available on their next turn.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Scripts\\r\\n\\r\\nAll of these scripts use network, so when running in the sandbox, request escalation when running them.\\r\\n\\r\\n- `scripts/list-skills.py` (prints skills list with installed annotations)\\r\\n- `scripts/list-skills.py --format json`\\r\\n- Example (experimental list): `scripts/list-skills.py --path skills/.experimental`\\r\\n- `scripts/install-skill-from-github.py --repo <owner>/<repo> --path <path/to/skill> [<path/to/skill> ...]`\\r\\n- `scripts/install-skill-from-github.py --url https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/tree/<ref>/<path>`\\r\\n- Example (experimental skill): `scripts/install-skill-from-github.py --repo openai/skills --path skills/.experimental/<skill-name>`\\r\\n\\r\\n## Behavior and Options\\r\\n\\r\\n- Defaults to direct download for public GitHub repos.\\r\\n- If download fails with auth/permission errors, falls back to git sparse checkout.\\r\\n- Aborts if the destination skill directory already exists.\\r\\n- Installs into `$CODEX_HOME/skills/<skill-name>` (defaults to `~/.codex/skills`).\\r\\n- Multiple `--path` values install multiple skills in one run, each named from the path basename unless `--name` is supplied.\\r\\n- Options: `--ref <ref>` (default `main`), `--dest <path>`, `--method auto|download|git`.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Notes\\r\\n\\r\\n- Curated listing is fetched from `https://github.com/openai/skills/tree/main/skills/.curated` via the GitHub API. If it is unavailable, explain the error and exit.\\r\\n- Private GitHub repos can be accessed via existing git credentials or optional `GITHUB_TOKEN`/`GH_TOKEN` for download.\\r\\n- Git fallback tries HTTPS first, then SSH.\\r\\n- The skills at https://github.com/openai/skills/tree/main/skills/.system are preinstalled, so no need to help users install those. If they ask, just explain this. If they insist, you can download and overwrite.\\r\\n- Installed annotations come from `$CODEX_HOME/skills`.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\nFILE C:\\\\Users\\\\Joshu\\\\dev\\\\ai-os\\\\skills\\\\codex\\\\superwhisper\\\\SKILL.md\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: superwhisper\\r\\ndescription: Maintain Joshua\'s Superwhisper dictation setup on this Windows laptop. Use for vocabulary requests, spoken correction mappings, custom modes, transcript-error scans, configuration checks, or restarting Superwhisper.\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Superwhisper\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source of truth is `C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/superwhisper/`. Read\\r\\n`superwhisper/CLAUDE.md` before changing anything; despite its name, it contains the\\r\\napp-specific operating rules for both runtimes.\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua uses Left Alt to toggle recording. Preserve it and verify it after restart. Complete configuration changes, sync them, restart\\r\\nthe app silently, and verify what loaded without opening Superwhisper or Settings.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Correction or vocabulary request\\r\\n\\r\\n- `X --> Y`, \\"replace X with Y\\", and \\"X should always be Y\\" add rows to\\r\\n  `superwhisper/replacements.md`. Matching is case-insensitive.\\r\\n- \\"Save X in my vocabulary\\" adds X to `superwhisper/vocabulary.md` only when X is an\\r\\n  unusual name or domain term the voice model needs help recognizing.\\r\\n- Do not automatically add replacement targets to vocabulary. That experiment expanded\\r\\n  the list to 654 entries on 2026-09-11 and immediately worsened transcription. Keep the\\r\\n  vocabulary around 40 terms.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor a replacement, add useful variants in the same pass: the exact error, a trailing-period\\r\\nform for one-word dictation, plausible phonetic spellings, joined or split words, and spoken\\r\\npunctuation such as \\"dot\\" or \\"at\\". Add only variants that plausibly identify the intended\\r\\nterm. Never replace an ordinary word such as `seven`, `white`, or `care` merely because it\\r\\nresembles a name; that would corrupt normal sentences.\\r\\n\\r\\nUse `apply_patch` for vault edits. Preserve the Markdown table format:\\r\\n\\r\\n```markdown\\r\\n| heard form | Wanted form | YYYY-MM-DD | reason |\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nAfter editing, run from `C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/superwhisper/`:\\r\\n\\r\\n```powershell\\r\\npython sync.py --restart\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nReport the final loaded counts. If the loaded mode count is below the number of mode files,\\r\\nfix the rejected mode before reporting success.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Custom mode\\r\\n\\r\\nRead the relevant existing file in `superwhisper/modes/` and copy its structure into a new\\r\\n`modes/<key>.md` file. Frontmatter controls the model and context; the body is the prompt.\\r\\n\\r\\n- Use S1-Voice (`sv-1`) unless Joshua chooses another voice model.\\r\\n- The app picker and the app\'s mode JSON are the authority for available language models.\\r\\n  Website documentation can lag. Never infer a model ID.\\r\\n- Agent-output modes need an explicit \\"you are not an assistant\\" instruction so the model\\r\\n  cleans the dictated request rather than answering it.\\r\\n- Student-facing modes must follow `wiki/teaching-voice.md`.\\r\\n- Enable only the context the mode needs.\\r\\n- Put worked examples under `## Examples`; `sync.py` folds them into prompt text because\\r\\n  externally written `promptExamples` cause the app to reject a mode.\\r\\n\\r\\nAfter adding a mode, update the mode table in `superwhisper/CLAUDE.md`, then sync, restart,\\r\\nand verify the loaded `modeKeys`.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Transcript scan\\r\\n\\r\\nRun one of:\\r\\n\\r\\n```powershell\\r\\npython C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/superwhisper/scan.py\\r\\npython C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/superwhisper/scan.py --since 7\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThe report is written to `superwhisper/research/SCAN-<date>.md`. Apply safe, specific\\r\\nmis-hearing fixes. Report risky suggestions separately and leave them unapplied. A common\\r\\nEnglish word is always a risky replacement target.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Operational constraints\\r\\n\\r\\n- Edit the vault files, not the app JSON. `sync.py` owns the generated JSON.\\r\\n- The real app data is under\\r\\n  `C:/Users/Joshu/AppData/Local/com.superwhisper.app/`; `sync.py` already uses the tested\\r\\n  path and restart procedure.\\r\\n- Do not launch the executable directly and do not open visible app windows. Use\\r\\n  `sync.py --restart`.\\r\\n- The app reads configuration only at launch. A successful write is not proof; the final\\r\\n  `modeKeys` readback after restart is proof.\\r\\n- Apply individual corrections immediately rather than batching them for later.\\r\\n- Append a short entry to `wiki/SUPERWHISPER-DICTIONARY.md` only for notable policy,\\r\\n  mode, migration, or bulk-scan changes. Routine one-word replacements do not need a ledger\\r\\n  entry.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\nFILE C:\\\\Users\\\\Joshu\\\\dev\\\\ai-os\\\\skills\\\\codex\\\\test-driven-development\\\\SKILL.md\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: test-driven-development\\r\\ndescription: Use when implementing any feature or bugfix, before writing implementation code\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Test-Driven Development (TDD)\\r\\n\\r\\n## Overview\\r\\n\\r\\nWrite the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Core principle:** If you didn\'t watch the test fail, you don\'t know if it tests the right thing.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**\\r\\n\\r\\n## When to Use\\r\\n\\r\\n**Always:**\\r\\n- New features\\r\\n- Bug fixes\\r\\n- Refactoring\\r\\n- Behavior changes\\r\\n\\r\\n**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**\\r\\n- Throwaway prototypes\\r\\n- Generated code\\r\\n- Configuration files\\r\\n\\r\\nThinking \\"skip TDD just this once\\"? Stop. That\'s rationalization.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Anti-Pattern: Horizontal Slices\\r\\n\\r\\n**DO NOT write all tests first, then all implementation.** This is \\"horizontal slicing\\" — treating RED as \\"write all tests\\" and GREEN as \\"write all code.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\nThis produces **crap tests**:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Tests written in bulk test _imagined_ behavior, not _actual_ behavior\\r\\n- You end up testing the _shape_ of things (data structures, function signatures) rather than user-facing behavior\\r\\n- Tests become insensitive to real changes — they pass when behavior breaks, fail when behavior is fine\\r\\n- You outrun your headlights, committing to test structure before understanding the implementation\\r\\n\\r\\n**Correct approach:** Vertical slices via tracer bullets. One test → one implementation → repeat. Each test responds to what you learned from the previous cycle.\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\nWRONG (horizontal):\\r\\n  RED:   test1, test2, test3, test4, test5\\r\\n  GREEN: impl1, impl2, impl3, impl4, impl5\\r\\n\\r\\nRIGHT (vertical):\\r\\n  RED→GREEN: test1→impl1\\r\\n  RED→GREEN: test2→impl2\\r\\n  RED→GREEN: test3→impl3\\r\\n  ...\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nSee [tests.md](tests.md) for good/bad test examples, [mocking.md](mocking.md) for mocking guidelines, and [refactoring.md](refactoring.md) for refactor candidates.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The Iron Law\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\nNO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nWrite code before the test? Delete it. Start over.\\r\\n\\r\\n**No exceptions:**\\r\\n- Don\'t keep it as \\"reference\\"\\r\\n- Don\'t \\"adapt\\" it while writing tests\\r\\n- Don\'t look at it\\r\\n- Delete means delete\\r\\n\\r\\nImplement fresh from tests. Period.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Red-Green-Refactor\\r\\n\\r\\n```dot\\r\\ndigraph tdd_cycle {\\r\\n    rankdir=LR;\\r\\n    red [label=\\"RED\\\\nWrite failing test\\", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=\\"#ffcccc\\"];\\r\\n    verify_red [label=\\"Verify fails\\\\ncorrectly\\", shape=diamond];\\r\\n    green [label=\\"GREEN\\\\nMinimal code\\", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=\\"#ccffcc\\"];\\r\\n    verify_green [label=\\"Verify passes\\\\nAll green\\", shape=diamond];\\r\\n    refactor [label=\\"REFACTOR\\\\nClean up\\", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=\\"#ccccff\\"];\\r\\n    next [label=\\"Next\\", shape=ellipse];\\r\\n\\r\\n    red -> verify_red;\\r\\n    verify_red -> green [label=\\"yes\\"];\\r\\n    verify_red -> red [label=\\"wrong\\\\nfailure\\"];\\r\\n    green -> verify_green;\\r\\n    verify_green -> refactor [label=\\"yes\\"];\\r\\n    verify_green -> green [label=\\"no\\"];\\r\\n    refactor -> verify_green [label=\\"stay\\\\ngreen\\"];\\r\\n    verify_green -> next;\\r\\n    next -> red;\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n### RED - Write Failing Test\\r\\n\\r\\nWrite one minimal test showing what should happen.\\r\\n\\r\\n<Good>\\r\\n```typescript\\r\\ntest(\'retries failed operations 3 times\', async () => {\\r\\n  let attempts = 0;\\r\\n  const operation = () => {\\r\\n    attempts++;\\r\\n    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error(\'fail\');\\r\\n    return \'success\';\\r\\n  };\\r\\n\\r\\n  const result = await retryOperation(operation);\\r\\n\\r\\n  expect(result).toBe(\'success\');\\r\\n  expect(attempts).toBe(3);\\r\\n});\\r\\n```\\r\\nClear name, tests real behavior, one thing\\r\\n</Good>\\r\\n\\r\\n<Bad>\\r\\n```typescript\\r\\ntest(\'retry works\', async () => {\\r\\n  const mock = jest.fn()\\r\\n    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())\\r\\n    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())\\r\\n    .mockResolvedValueOnce(\'success\');\\r\\n  await retryOperation(mock);\\r\\n  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);\\r\\n});\\r\\n```\\r\\nVague name, tests mock not code\\r\\n</Bad>\\r\\n\\r\\n**Requirements:**\\r\\n- One behavior\\r\\n- Clear name\\r\\n- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)\\r\\n\\r\\n### Verify RED - Watch It Fail\\r\\n\\r\\n**MANDATORY. Never skip.**\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\nnpm test path/to/test.test.ts\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nConfirm:\\r\\n- Test fails (not errors)\\r\\n- Failure message is expected\\r\\n- Fails because feature missing (not typos)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Test passes?** You\'re testing existing behavior. Fix test.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.\\r\\n\\r\\n### GREEN - Minimal Code\\r\\n\\r\\nWrite simplest code to pass the test.\\r\\n\\r\\n<Good>\\r\\n```typescript\\r\\nasync function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {\\r\\n  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {\\r\\n    try {\\r\\n      return await fn();\\r\\n    } catch (e) {\\r\\n      if (i === 2) throw e;\\r\\n    }\\r\\n  }\\r\\n  throw new Error(\'unreachable\');\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\nJust enough to pass\\r\\n</Good>\\r\\n\\r\\n<Bad>\\r\\n```typescript\\r\\nasync function retryOperation<T>(\\r\\n  fn: () => Promise<T>,\\r\\n  options?: {\\r\\n    maxRetries?: number;\\r\\n    backoff?: \'linear\' | \'exponential\';\\r\\n    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;\\r\\n  }\\r\\n): Promise<T> {\\r\\n  // YAGNI\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\nOver-engineered\\r\\n</Bad>\\r\\n\\r\\nDon\'t add features, refactor other code, or \\"improve\\" beyond the test.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass\\r\\n\\r\\n**MANDATORY.**\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\nnpm test path/to/test.test.ts\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nConfirm:\\r\\n- Test passes\\r\\n- Other tests still pass\\r\\n- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Other tests fail?** Fix now.\\r\\n\\r\\n### REFACTOR - Clean Up\\r\\n\\r\\nAfter green only:\\r\\n- Remove duplication\\r\\n- Improve names\\r\\n- Extract helpers\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep tests green. Don\'t add behavior. See [refactoring.md](refactoring.md) for the full list of refactor candidates.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Repeat\\r\\n\\r\\nNext failing test for next feature.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Good Tests\\r\\n\\r\\n| Quality | Good | Bad |\\r\\n|---------|------|-----|\\r\\n| **Minimal** | One thing. \\"and\\" in name? Split it. | `test(\'validates email and domain and whitespace\')` |\\r\\n| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test(\'test1\')` |\\r\\n| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |\\r\\n\\r\\n## Why Order Matters\\r\\n\\r\\n**\\"I\'ll write tests after to verify it works\\"**\\r\\n\\r\\nTests written after code pass immediately. Passing immediately proves nothing:\\r\\n- Might test wrong thing\\r\\n- Might test implementation, not behavior\\r\\n- Might miss edge cases you forgot\\r\\n- You never saw it catch the bug\\r\\n\\r\\nTest-first forces you to see the test fail, proving it actually tests something.\\r\\n\\r\\n**\\"I already manually tested all the edge cases\\"**\\r\\n\\r\\nManual testing is ad-hoc. You think you tested everything but:\\r\\n- No record of what you tested\\r\\n- Can\'t re-run when code changes\\r\\n- Easy to forget cases under pressure\\r\\n- \\"It worked when I tried it\\" ≠ comprehensive\\r\\n\\r\\nAutomated tests are systematic. They run the same way every time.\\r\\n\\r\\n**\\"Deleting X hours of work is wasteful\\"**\\r\\n\\r\\nSunk cost fallacy. The time is already gone. Your choice now:\\r\\n- Delete and rewrite with TDD (X more hours, high confidence)\\r\\n- Keep it and add tests after (30 min, low confidence, likely bugs)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe \\"waste\\" is keeping code you can\'t trust. Working code without real tests is technical debt.\\r\\n\\r\\n**\\"TDD is dogmatic, being pragmatic means adapting\\"**\\r\\n\\r\\nTDD IS pragmatic:\\r\\n- Finds bugs before commit (faster than debugging after)\\r\\n- Prevents regressions (tests catch breaks immediately)\\r\\n- Documents behavior (tests show how to use code)\\r\\n- Enables refactoring (change freely, tests catch breaks)\\r\\n\\r\\n\\"Pragmatic\\" shortcuts = debugging in production = slower.\\r\\n\\r\\n**\\"Tests after achieve the same goals - it\'s spirit not ritual\\"**\\r\\n\\r\\nNo. Tests-after answer \\"What does this do?\\" Tests-first answer \\"What should this do?\\"\\r\\n\\r\\nTests-after are biased by your implementation. You test what you built, not what\'s required. You verify remembered edge cases, not discovered ones.\\r\\n\\r\\nTests-first force edge case discovery before implementing. Tests-after verify you remembered everything (you didn\'t).\\r\\n\\r\\n30 minutes of tests after ≠ TDD. You get coverage, lose proof tests work.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Common Rationalizations\\r\\n\\r\\n| Excuse | Reality |\\r\\n|--------|---------|\\r\\n| \\"Too simple to test\\" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |\\r\\n| \\"I\'ll test after\\" | Tests passing immediately prove nothing. |\\r\\n| \\"Tests after achieve same goals\\" | Tests-after = \\"what does this do?\\" Tests-first = \\"what should this do?\\" |\\r\\n| \\"Already manually tested\\" | Ad-hoc ≠ systematic. No record, can\'t re-run. |\\r\\n| \\"Deleting X hours is wasteful\\" | Sunk cost fallacy. Keeping unverified code is technical debt. |\\r\\n| \\"Keep as reference, write tests first\\" | You\'ll adapt it. That\'s testing after. Delete means delete. |\\r\\n| \\"Need to explore first\\" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |\\r\\n| \\"Test hard = design unclear\\" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |\\r\\n| \\"TDD will slow me down\\" | TDD faster than debugging. Pragmatic = test-first. |\\r\\n| \\"Manual test faster\\" | Manual doesn\'t prove edge cases. You\'ll re-test every change. |\\r\\n| \\"Existing code has no tests\\" | You\'re improving it. Add tests for existing code. |\\r\\n\\r\\n## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over\\r\\n\\r\\n- Code before test\\r\\n- Test after implementation\\r\\n- Test passes immediately\\r\\n- Can\'t explain why test failed\\r\\n- Tests added \\"later\\"\\r\\n- Rationalizing \\"just this once\\"\\r\\n- \\"I already manually tested it\\"\\r\\n- \\"Tests after achieve the same purpose\\"\\r\\n- \\"It\'s about spirit not ritual\\"\\r\\n- \\"Keep as reference\\" or \\"adapt existing code\\"\\r\\n- \\"Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful\\"\\r\\n- \\"TDD is dogmatic, I\'m being pragmatic\\"\\r\\n- \\"This is different because...\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**\\r\\n\\r\\n## Example: Bug Fix\\r\\n\\r\\n**Bug:** Empty email accepted\\r\\n\\r\\n**RED**\\r\\n```typescript\\r\\ntest(\'rejects empty email\', async () => {\\r\\n  const result = await submitForm({ email: \'\' });\\r\\n  expect(result.error).toBe(\'Email required\');\\r\\n});\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**Verify RED**\\r\\n```bash\\r\\n$ npm test\\r\\nFAIL: expected \'Email required\', got undefined\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**GREEN**\\r\\n```typescript\\r\\nfunction submitForm(data: FormData) {\\r\\n  if (!data.email?.trim()) {\\r\\n    return { error: \'Email required\' };\\r\\n  }\\r\\n  // ...\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**Verify GREEN**\\r\\n```bash\\r\\n$ npm test\\r\\nPASS\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**REFACTOR**\\r\\nExtract validation for multiple fields if needed.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Verification Checklist\\r\\n\\r\\nBefore marking work complete:\\r\\n\\r\\n- [ ] Every new function/method has a test\\r\\n- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing\\r\\n- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)\\r\\n- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test\\r\\n- [ ] All tests pass\\r\\n- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)\\r\\n- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)\\r\\n- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered\\r\\n\\r\\nCan\'t check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.\\r\\n\\r\\n## When Stuck\\r\\n\\r\\n| Problem | Solution |\\r\\n|---------|----------|\\r\\n| Don\'t know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |\\r\\n| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |\\r\\n| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |\\r\\n| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |\\r\\n\\r\\n## Debugging Integration\\r\\n\\r\\nBug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.\\r\\n\\r\\nNever fix bugs without a test.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Testing Anti-Patterns\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen adding mocks or test utilities, read [testing-anti-patterns.md](testing-anti-patterns.md) to avoid common pitfalls:\\r\\n- Testing mock behavior instead of real behavior\\r\\n- Adding test-only methods to production classes\\r\\n- Mocking without understanding dependencies\\r\\n\\r\\n## Final Rule\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\nProduction code → test exists and failed first\\r\\nOtherwise → not TDD\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nNo exceptions without your human partner\'s permission.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\nFILE C:\\\\Users\\\\Joshu\\\\dev\\\\ai-os\\\\skills\\\\codex\\\\to-prd\\\\SKILL.md\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: to-prd\\r\\ndescription: Turn the current conversation into a PRD and publish it to the project issue tracker — no interview, just synthesis of what you\'ve already discussed.\\r\\ndisable-model-invocation: true\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\nThis skill takes the current conversation context and codebase understanding and produces a PRD. Do NOT interview the user — just synthesize what you already know.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe issue tracker and triage label vocabulary should have been provided to you — run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` if not.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Process\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Explore the repo to understand the current state of the codebase, if you haven\'t already. Use the project\'s domain glossary vocabulary throughout the PRD, and respect any ADRs in the area you\'re touching.\\r\\n\\r\\n2. Sketch out the seams at which you\'re going to test the feature. Existing seams should be preferred to new ones. Use the highest seam possible. If new seams are needed, propose them at the highest point you can. The fewer seams across the codebase, the better - the ideal number is one.\\r\\n\\r\\nCheck with the user that these seams match their expectations.\\r\\n\\r\\n3. Write the PRD using the template below, then publish it to the project issue tracker. Apply the `ready-for-agent` triage label - no need for additional triage.\\r\\n\\r\\n<prd-template>\\r\\n\\r\\n## Problem Statement\\r\\n\\r\\nThe problem that the user is facing, from the user\'s perspective.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Solution\\r\\n\\r\\nThe solution to the problem, from the user\'s perspective.\\r\\n\\r\\n## User Stories\\r\\n\\r\\nA LONG, numbered list of user stories. Each user story should be in the format of:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. As an <actor>, I want a <feature>, so that <benefit>\\r\\n\\r\\n<user-story-example>\\r\\n1. As a mobile bank customer, I want to see balance on my accounts, so that I can make better informed decisions about my spending\\r\\n</user-story-example>\\r\\n\\r\\nThis list of user stories should be extremely extensive and cover all aspects of the feature.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Implementation Decisions\\r\\n\\r\\nA list of implementation decisions that were made. This can include:\\r\\n\\r\\n- The modules that will be built/modified\\r\\n- The interfaces of those modules that will be modified\\r\\n- Technical clarifications from the developer\\r\\n- Architectural decisions\\r\\n- Schema changes\\r\\n- API contracts\\r\\n- Specific interactions\\r\\n\\r\\nDo NOT include specific file paths or code snippets. They may end up being outdated very quickly.\\r\\n\\r\\nException: if a prototype produced a snippet that encodes a decision more precisely than prose can (state machine, reducer, schema, type shape), inline it within the relevant decision and note briefly that it came from a prototype. Trim to the decision-rich parts — not a working demo, just the important bits.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Testing Decisions\\r\\n\\r\\nA list of testing decisions that were made. Include:\\r\\n\\r\\n- A description of what makes a good test (only test external behavior, not implementation details)\\r\\n- Which modules will be tested\\r\\n- Prior art for the tests (i.e. similar types of tests in the codebase)\\r\\n\\r\\n## Out of Scope\\r\\n\\r\\nA description of the things that are out of scope for this PRD.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Further Notes\\r\\n\\r\\nAny further notes about the feature.\\r\\n\\r\\n</prd-template>\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\nFILE C:\\\\Users\\\\Joshu\\\\dev\\\\ai-os\\\\skills\\\\codex\\\\using-git-worktrees\\\\SKILL.md\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: using-git-worktrees\\r\\ndescription: Use when starting feature work that needs isolation from current workspace or before executing implementation plans - ensures an isolated workspace exists via native tools or git worktree fallback\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Using Git Worktrees\\r\\n\\r\\n## Overview\\r\\n\\r\\nEnsure work happens in an isolated workspace. Prefer your platform\'s native worktree tools. Fall back to manual git worktrees only when no native tool is available.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Core principle:** Detect existing isolation first. Then use native tools. Then fall back to git. Never fight the harness.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Announce at start:** \\"I\'m using the using-git-worktrees skill to set up an isolated workspace.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n## Step 0: Detect Existing Isolation\\r\\n\\r\\n**Before creating anything, check if you are already in an isolated workspace.**\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\nGIT_DIR=$(cd \\"$(git rev-parse --git-dir)\\" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)\\r\\nGIT_COMMON=$(cd \\"$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)\\" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)\\r\\nBRANCH=$(git branch --show-current)\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**Submodule guard:** `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON` is also true inside git submodules. Before concluding \\"already in a worktree,\\" verify you are not in a submodule:\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\n# If this returns a path, you\'re in a submodule, not a worktree — treat as normal repo\\r\\ngit rev-parse --show-superproject-working-tree 2>/dev/null\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**If `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON` (and not a submodule):** You are already in a linked worktree. Skip to Step 2 (Project Setup). Do NOT create another worktree.\\r\\n\\r\\nReport with branch state:\\r\\n- On a branch: \\"Already in isolated workspace at `<path>` on branch `<name>`.\\"\\r\\n- Detached HEAD: \\"Already in isolated workspace at `<path>` (detached HEAD, externally managed). Branch creation needed at finish time.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n**If `GIT_DIR == GIT_COMMON` (or in a submodule):** You are in a normal repo checkout.\\r\\n\\r\\nHas the user already indicated their worktree preference in your instructions? If not, ask for consent before creating a worktree:\\r\\n\\r\\n> \\"Would you like me to set up an isolated worktree? It protects your current branch from changes.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\nHonor any existing declared preference without asking. If the user declines consent, work in place and skip to Step 2.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Step 1: Create Isolated Workspace\\r\\n\\r\\n**You have two mechanisms. Try them in this order.**\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1a. Native Worktree Tools (preferred)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe user has asked for an isolated workspace (Step 0 consent). Do you already have a way to create a worktree? It might be a tool with a name like `EnterWorktree`, `WorktreeCreate`, a `/worktree` command, or a `--worktree` flag. If you do, use it and skip to Step 2.\\r\\n\\r\\nNative tools handle directory placement, branch creation, and cleanup automatically. Using `git worktree add` when you have a native tool creates phantom state your harness can\'t see or manage.\\r\\n\\r\\nOnly proceed to Step 1b if you have no native worktree tool available.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1b. Git Worktree Fallback\\r\\n\\r\\n**Only use this if Step 1a does not apply** — you have no native worktree tool available. Create a worktree manually using git.\\r\\n\\r\\n#### Directory Selection\\r\\n\\r\\nFollow this priority order. Explicit user preference always beats observed filesystem state.\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Check your instructions for a declared worktree directory preference.** If the user has already specified one, use it without asking.\\r\\n\\r\\n2. **Check for an existing project-local worktree directory:**\\r\\n   ```bash\\r\\n   ls -d .worktrees 2>/dev/null     # Preferred (hidden)\\r\\n   ls -d worktrees 2>/dev/null      # Alternative\\r\\n   ```\\r\\n   If found, use it. If both exist, `.worktrees` wins.\\r\\n\\r\\n3. **If there is no other guidance available**, default to `.worktrees/` at the project root.\\r\\n\\r\\n#### Safety Verification (project-local directories only)\\r\\n\\r\\n**MUST verify directory is ignored before creating worktree:**\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\ngit check-ignore -q .worktrees 2>/dev/null || git check-ignore -q worktrees 2>/dev/null\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**If NOT ignored:** Add to .gitignore, commit the change, then proceed.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Why critical:** Prevents accidentally committing worktree contents to repository.\\r\\n\\r\\n#### Create the Worktree\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\n# Determine path based on chosen location\\r\\npath=\\"$LOCATION/$BRANCH_NAME\\"\\r\\n\\r\\ngit worktree add \\"$path\\" -b \\"$BRANCH_NAME\\"\\r\\ncd \\"$path\\"\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**Sandbox fallback:** If `git worktree add` fails with a permission error (sandbox denial), tell the user the sandbox blocked worktree creation and you\'re working in the current directory instead. Then run setup and baseline tests in place.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Step 2: Project Setup\\r\\n\\r\\nAuto-detect and run appropriate setup:\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\n# Node.js\\r\\nif [ -f package.json ]; then npm install; fi\\r\\n\\r\\n# Rust\\r\\nif [ -f Cargo.toml ]; then cargo build; fi\\r\\n\\r\\n# Python\\r\\nif [ -f requirements.txt ]; then pip install -r requirements.txt; fi\\r\\nif [ -f pyproject.toml ]; then poetry install; fi\\r\\n\\r\\n# Go\\r\\nif [ -f go.mod ]; then go mod download; fi\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n## Step 3: Verify Clean Baseline\\r\\n\\r\\nRun tests to ensure workspace starts clean:\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\n# Use project-appropriate command\\r\\nnpm test / cargo test / pytest / go test ./...\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**If tests fail:** Report failures, ask whether to proceed or investigate.\\r\\n\\r\\n**If tests pass:** Report ready.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Report\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\nWorktree ready at <full-path>\\r\\nTests passing (<N> tests, 0 failures)\\r\\nReady to implement <feature-name>\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n## Quick Reference\\r\\n\\r\\n| Situation | Action |\\r\\n|-----------|--------|\\r\\n| Already in linked worktree | Skip creation (Step 0) |\\r\\n| In a submodule | Treat as normal repo (Step 0 guard) |\\r\\n| Native worktree tool available | Use it (Step 1a) |\\r\\n| No native tool | Git worktree fallback (Step 1b) |\\r\\n| `.worktrees/` exists | Use it (verify ignored) |\\r\\n| `worktrees/` exists | Use it (verify ignored) |\\r\\n| Both exist | Use `.worktrees/` |\\r\\n| Neither exists | Check instruction file, then default `.worktrees/` |\\r\\n| Directory not ignored | Add to .gitignore + commit |\\r\\n| Permission error on create | Sandbox fallback, work in place |\\r\\n| Tests fail during baseline | Report failures + ask |\\r\\n| No package.json/Cargo.toml | Skip dependency install |\\r\\n\\r\\n## Common Mistakes\\r\\n\\r\\n### Fighting the harness\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Problem:** Using `git worktree add` when the platform already provides isolation\\r\\n- **Fix:** Step 0 detects existing isolation. Step 1a defers to native tools.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Skipping detection\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Problem:** Creating a nested worktree inside an existing one\\r\\n- **Fix:** Always run Step 0 before creating anything\\r\\n\\r\\n### Skipping ignore verification\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Problem:** Worktree contents get tracked, pollute git status\\r\\n- **Fix:** Always use `git check-ignore` before creating project-local worktree\\r\\n\\r\\n### Assuming directory location\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Problem:** Creates inconsistency, violates project conventions\\r\\n- **Fix:** Follow priority: explicit instructions > existing project-local directory > default\\r\\n\\r\\n### Proceeding with failing tests\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Problem:** Can\'t distinguish new bugs from pre-existing issues\\r\\n- **Fix:** Report failures, get explicit permission to proceed\\r\\n\\r\\n## Red Flags\\r\\n\\r\\n**Never:**\\r\\n- Create a worktree when Step 0 detects existing isolation\\r\\n- Use `git worktree add` when you have a native worktree tool (e.g., `EnterWorktree`). This is the #1 mistake — if you have it, use it.\\r\\n- Skip Step 1a by jumping straight to Step 1b\'s git commands\\r\\n- Create worktree without verifying it\'s ignored (project-local)\\r\\n- Skip baseline test verification\\r\\n- Proceed with failing tests without asking\\r\\n\\r\\n**Always:**\\r\\n- Run Step 0 detection first\\r\\n- Prefer native tools over git fallback\\r\\n- Follow directory priority: explicit instructions > existing project-local directory > default\\r\\n- Verify directory is ignored for project-local\\r\\n- Auto-detect and run project setup\\r\\n- Verify clean test baseline\\r\\n\\r\\n"}'}]

Matching is case-insensitive.\\r\\n- \\"Save X in my vocabulary\\" adds X to `superwhisper/vocabulary.md` only when X is an\\r\\n  unusual name or domain term the voice model needs help recognizing.\\r\\n- Do not automatically add replacement targets to vocabulary. Keep the\\r\\n  vocabulary around 40 terms.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor a replacement, add useful variants in the same pass: the exact error, a trailing-period\\r\\nform for one-word dictation, plausible phonetic spellings, joined or split words, and spoken\\r\\npunctuation such as \\"dot\\" or \\"at\\".
