[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 8.2 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"5865f3","wall_time_seconds":0.8210734,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":6460,"output":"\\r\\n### skills\\\\claude\\\\playground\\\\SKILL.md\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: playground\\r\\ndescription: Creates interactive HTML playgrounds — self-contained single-file explorers that let users configure something visually through controls, see a live preview, and copy out a prompt. Use when the user asks to make a playground, explorer, or interactive tool for a topic.\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Playground Builder\\r\\n\\r\\nA playground is a self-contained HTML file with interactive controls on one side, a live preview on the other, and a prompt output at the bottom with a copy button. The user adjusts controls, explores visually, then copies the generated prompt back into Claude.\\r\\n\\r\\n## When to use this skill\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen the user asks for an interactive playground, explorer, or visual tool for a topic — especially when the input space is large, visual, or structural and hard to express as plain text.\\r\\n\\r\\n## How to use this skill\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Identify the playground type** from the user\'s request\\r\\n2. **Load the matching template** from `templates/`:\\r\\n   - `templates/design-playground.md` — Visual design decisions (components, layouts, spacing, color, typography)\\r\\n   - `templates/data-explorer.md` — Data and query building (SQL, APIs, pipelines, regex)\\r\\n   - `templates/concept-map.md` — Learning and exploration (concept maps, knowledge gaps, scope mapping)\\r\\n   - `templates/document-critique.md` — Document review (suggestions with approve/reject/comment workflow)\\r\\n   - `templates/diff-review.md` — Code review (git diffs, commits, PRs with line-by-line commenting)\\r\\n   - `templates/code-map.md` — Codebase architecture (component relationships, data flow, layer diagrams)\\r\\n3. **Follow the template** to build the playground. If the topic doesn\'t fit any template cleanly, use the one closest and adapt.\\r\\n4. **Open in browser.** After writing the HTML file, run `open <filename>.html` to launch it in the user\'s default browser.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Core requirements (every playground)\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Single HTML file.** Inline all CSS and JS. No external dependencies.\\r\\n- **Live preview.** Updates instantly on every control change. No \\"Apply\\" button.\\r\\n- **Prompt output.** Natural language, not a value dump. Only mentions non-default choices. Includes enough context to act on without seeing the playground. Updates live.\\r\\n- **Copy button.** Clipboard copy with brief \\"Copied!\\" feedback.\\r\\n- **Sensible defaults + presets.** Looks good on first load. Include 3-5 named presets that snap all controls to a cohesive combination.\\r\\n- **Dark theme.** System font for UI, monospace for code/values. Minimal chrome.\\r\\n\\r\\n## State management pattern\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep a single state object. Every control writes to it, every render reads from it.\\r\\n\\r\\n```javascript\\r\\nconst state = { /* all configurable values */ };\\r\\n\\r\\nfunction updateAll() {\\r\\n  renderPreview(); // update the visual\\r\\n  updatePrompt();  // rebuild the prompt text\\r\\n}\\r\\n// Every control calls updateAll() on change\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n## Prompt output pattern\\r\\n\\r\\n```javascript\\r\\nfunction updatePrompt() {\\r\\n  const parts = [];\\r\\n\\r\\n  // Only mention non-default values\\r\\n  if (state.borderRadius !== DEFAULTS.borderRadius) {\\r\\n    parts.push(`border-radius of ${state.borderRadius}px`);\\r\\n  }\\r\\n\\r\\n  // Use qualitative language alongside numbers\\r\\n  if (state.shadowBlur > 16) parts.push(\'a pronounced shadow\');\\r\\n  else if (state.shadowBlur > 0) parts.push(\'a subtle shadow\');\\r\\n\\r\\n  prompt.textContent = `Update the card to use ${parts.join(\', \')}.`;\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n## Common mistakes to avoid\\r\\n\\r\\n- Prompt output is just a value dump → write it as a natural instruction\\r\\n- Too many controls at once → group by concern, hide advanced in a collapsible section\\r\\n- Preview doesn\'t update instantly → every control change must trigger immediate re-render\\r\\n- No defaults or presets → starts empty or broken on load\\r\\n- External dependencies → if CDN is down, playground is dead\\r\\n- Prompt lacks context → include enough that it\'s actionable without the playground\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n### skills\\\\claude\\\\ponytail\\\\SKILL.md\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: ponytail\\r\\ndescription: >\\r\\n  Forces the laziest solution that actually works, simplest, shortest, most\\r\\n  minimal. Channels a senior dev who has seen everything: question whether the\\r\\n  task needs to exist at all (YAGNI), reach for the standard library before\\r\\n  custom code, native platform features before dependencies, one line before\\r\\n  fifty. Supports intensity levels: lite, full (default), ultra. Use whenever\\r\\n  the user says \\"ponytail\\", \\"be lazy\\", \\"lazy mode\\", \\"simplest solution\\",\\r\\n  \\"minimal solution\\", \\"yagni\\", \\"do less\\", or \\"shortest path\\", and whenever\\r\\n  they complain about over-engineering, bloat, boilerplate, or unnecessary\\r\\n  dependencies.\\r\\nargument-hint: \\"[lite|full|ultra]\\"\\r\\nlicense: MIT\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Ponytail\\r\\n\\r\\nYou are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have\\r\\nseen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best\\r\\ncode is the code never written.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Persistence\\r\\n\\r\\nACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if\\r\\nunsure. Off only: \\"stop ponytail\\" / \\"normal mode\\". Default: **full**.\\r\\nSwitch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The ladder\\r\\n\\r\\nStop at the first rung that holds:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)\\r\\n2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what\'s a few files over is the most common slop.\\r\\n3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.\\r\\n4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type=\\"date\\">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.\\r\\n5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.\\r\\n6. **Can it be one line?** One line.\\r\\n7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you\\r\\nunderstand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it\\r\\ntouches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →\\r\\ntake the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the\\r\\nright one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you\\r\\nedit, grep every caller of the function you\'re about to touch. The lazy fix IS\\r\\nthe root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a\\r\\nguard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves\\r\\nevery sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Rules\\r\\n\\r\\n- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.\\r\\n- No boilerplate, no scaffolding \\"for later\\", later can scaffold for itself.\\r\\n- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.\\r\\n- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn\'t lazy, it\'s a second bug.\\r\\n- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, \\"Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so.\\" Never stall on an answer you can default.\\r\\n- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that\'s correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.\\r\\n- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Output\\r\\n\\r\\nCode first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.\\r\\nNo essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer\\r\\nthan the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a\\r\\nsimplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user\\r\\nexplicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,\\r\\ngive it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.\\r\\n\\r\\nPattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`\\r\\n\\r\\n## Intensity\\r\\n\\r\\n| Level | What change |\\r\\n|-------|------------|\\r\\n| **lite** | Build what\'s asked, but name the lazier alternative in one line. User picks. |\\r\\n| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |\\r\\n| **ultra** | YAGNI extremist. Deletion before addition. Ship the one-liner and challenge the rest of the requirement in the same breath. |\\r\\n\\r\\nExample: \\"Add a cache for these API responses.\\"\\r\\n- lite: \\"Done, cache added. FYI: `functools.lru_cache` covers this in one line if you\'d rather not own a cache class.\\"\\r\\n- full: \\"`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short.\\"\\r\\n- ultra: \\"No cache until a profiler says so. When it does: `@lru_cache`. A hand-rolled TTL cache class is a bug farm with a hit rate.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n## When NOT to be lazy\\r\\n\\r\\nNever simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling\\r\\nthat prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything\\r\\nexplicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no\\r\\nre-arguing.\\r\\n\\r\\nNever lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the\\r\\nsolution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the\\r\\nchange touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips\\r\\ncomprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as\\r\\nefficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.\\r\\n\\r\\nHardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor\\r\\nreads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not\\r\\njust less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can\'t see.\\r\\n\\r\\nLazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a\\r\\nloop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the\\r\\nsmallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based\\r\\n`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no\\r\\nfixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no\\r\\ntest, YAGNI applies to tests too.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Boundaries\\r\\n\\r\\nPonytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for\\r\\nterse prose). \\"stop ponytail\\" / \\"normal mode\\": revert. Level persists until\\r\\nchanged or session end.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe shortest path to done is the right path.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n### skills\\\\claude\\\\research-deep\\\\SKILL.md\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: research-deep\\r\\ndescription: Read research outline, launch independent agent for each item for deep research. Uncertain Value Skipping**\\r\\nSkip conditions:\\r\\n- Field value contains `[uncertain]` string\\r\\n- Field name is in `uncertain` array\\r\\n- Field value is None or empty string\\r\\n\\r\\n### Step 4: Execute Script\\r\\nRun `python {topic}/generate_report.py`\\r\\n\\r\\n## Output\\r\\n- `{topic}/generate_report.py` - Conversion script\\r\\n- `{topic}/report.md` - Summary report\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n### skills\\\\claude\\\\review\\\\SKILL.md\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: review\\r\\ndescription: Review the changes since a fixed point (commit, branch, tag, or merge-base) along two axes — Standards (does the code follow this repo\'s documented coding standards?) and Spec (does the code match what the originating issue/PRD asked for?). Runs both reviews in parallel sub-agents and reports them side by side. Use when the user wants to review a branch, a PR, work-in-progress changes, or asks to \\"review since X\\".\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\nTwo-axis review of the diff between `HEAD` and a fixed point the user supplies:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Standards** — does the code conform to this repo\'s documented coding standards?\\r\\n- **Spec** — does the code faithfully implement the originating issue / PRD / spec?\\r\\n\\r\\nBoth axes run as **parallel sub-agents** so they don\'t pollute each other\'s context, then this skill aggregates their findings.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe issue tracker should have been provided to you — run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` if `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md` is missing.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Process\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1. Pin the fixed point\\r\\n\\r\\nWhatever the user said is the fixed point — a commit SHA, branch name, tag, `main`, `HEAD~5`, etc. If they didn\'t specify one, ask for it.\\r\\n\\r\\nCapture the diff command once: `git diff <fixed-point>...HEAD` (three-dot, so the comparison is against the merge-base). Also note the list of commits via `git log <fixed-point>..HEAD --oneline`.\\r\\n\\r\\nBefore going further, confirm the fixed point resolves (`git rev-parse <fixed-point>`) and the diff is non-empty. A bad ref or empty diff should fail here — not inside two parallel sub-agents.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2. Identify the spec source\\r\\n\\r\\nLook for the originating spec, in this order:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Issue references in the commit messages (`#123`, `Closes #45`, GitLab `!67`, etc.) — fetch via the workflow in `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`.\\r\\n2. A path the user passed as an argument.\\r\\n3. A PRD/spec file under `docs/`, `specs/`, or `.scratch/` matching the branch name or feature.\\r\\n4. If nothing is found, ask the user where the spec is. Spawn both sub-agents in parallel\\r\\n\\r\\nSend a single message with two `Agent` tool calls. Cite the standard (file + the rule). Distinguish hard violations from judgement calls. Skip anything tooling enforces. Under 400 words.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n**Spec sub-agent prompt** — include:\\r\\n\\r\\n- The diff command and commit list.\\r\\n- The path or fetched contents of the spec.\\r\\n- The brief: \\"Report: (a) requirements the spec asked for that are missing or partial; (b) behaviour in the diff that wasn\'t asked for (scope creep); (c) requirements that look implemented but where the implementation looks wrong. Quote the spec line for each finding. Under 400 words.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\nIf the spec is missing, skip the Spec sub-agent and note this in the final report.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 5. Aggregate\\r\\n\\r\\nPresent the two reports under `## Standards` and `## Spec` headings, verbatim or lightly cleaned. Do **not** merge or rerank findings — the two axes are deliberately separate (see _Why two axes_).\\r\\n\\r\\nEnd with a one-line summary: total findings per axis, and the worst issue _within each axis_ (if any). Don\'t pick a single winner across axes — that\'s the reranking the separation exists to prevent.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Why two axes\\r\\n\\r\\nA change can pass one axis and fail the other:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Code that follows every standard but implements the wrong thing → **Standards pass, Spec fail.**\\r\\n- Code that does exactly what the issue asked but breaks the project\'s conventions → **Spec pass, Standards fail.**\\r\\n\\r\\nReporting them separately stops one axis from masking the other.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n### skills\\\\claude\\\\scaffold-exercises\\\\SKILL.md\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: scaffold-exercises\\r\\ndescription: Create exercise directory structures with sections, problems, solutions, and explainers that pass linting. Use when user wants to scaffold exercises, create exercise stubs, or set up a new course section.\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Scaffold Exercises\\r\\n\\r\\nCreate exercise directory structures that pass `pnpm ai-hero-cli internal lint`, then commit with `git commit`.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Directory naming\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Sections**: `XX-section-name/` inside `exercises/` (e.g., `01-retrieval-skill-building`)\\r\\n- **Exercises**: `XX.YY-exercise-name/` inside a section (e.g., `01.03-retrieval-with-bm25`)\\r\\n- Section number = `XX`, exercise number = `XX.YY`\\r\\n- Names are dash-case (lowercase, hyphens)\\r\\n\\r\\n## Exercise variants\\r\\n\\r\\nEach exercise needs at least one of these subfolders:\\r\\n\\r\\n- `problem/` - student workspace with TODOs\\r\\n- `solution/` - reference implementation\\r\\n- `explainer/` - conceptual material, no TODOs\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen stubbing, default to `explainer/` unless the plan specifies otherwise.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Required files\\r\\n\\r\\nEach subfolder (`problem/`, `solution/`, `explainer/`) needs a `readme.md` that:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Is **not empty** (must have real content, even a single title line works)\\r\\n- Has no broken links\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen stubbing, create a minimal readme with a title and a description:\\r\\n\\r\\n```md\\r\\n# Exercise Title\\r\\n\\r\\nDescription here\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nIf the subfolder has code, it also needs a `main.ts` (>1 line). But for stubs, a readme-only exercise is fine.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Workflow\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Parse the plan** - extract section names, exercise names, and variant types\\r\\n2. **Create directories** - `mkdir -p` for each path\\r\\n3. **Create stub readmes** - one `readme.md` per variant folder with a title\\r\\n4. **Run lint** - `pnpm ai-hero-cli internal lint` to validate\\r\\n5. **Fix any errors** - iterate until lint passes\\r\\n\\r\\n## Lint rules summary\\r\\n\\r\\nThe linter (`pnpm ai-hero-cli internal lint`) checks:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Each exercise has subfolders (`problem/`, `solution/`, `explainer/`)\\r\\n- At least one of `problem/`, `explainer/`, or `explainer.1/` exists\\r\\n- `readme.md` exists and is non-empty in the primary subfolder\\r\\n- No `.gitkeep` files\\r\\n- No `speaker-notes.md` files\\r\\n- No broken links in readmes\\r\\n- No `pnpm run exercise` commands in readmes\\r\\n- `main.ts` required per subfolder unless it\'s readme-only\\r\\n\\r\\n## Moving/renaming exercises\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen renumbering or moving exercises:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Use `git mv` (not `mv`) to rename directories - preserves git history\\r\\n2. Update the numeric prefix to maintain order\\r\\n3. Drafts by default; sends only on an explicit go-ahead.\\r\\nallowed-tools: Bash Read Write Edit Glob Grep\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Send booking link\\r\\n\\r\\nFour steps that were being done by hand, seven times in a single session:\\r\\nlook up the email, draft in Joshua\'s voice, send, log the open loop. This does\\r\\nall four, in order, for one student or a batch.\\r\\n\\r\\n## 1. Look up — never guess an address\\r\\n\\r\\nThe roster is generated; rebuild it first so it reflects current folders.\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\npython3 system/scripts/build-roster.py\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThen read `students/roster.generated.md` for the student\'s **email** and\\r\\n**booking link**. Both must be present before drafting.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **No email recorded** → stop. Do not guess, do not search for a plausible\\r\\n  address. Tell Joshua the student\'s page has no `email:` in frontmatter.\\r\\n- **No booking pass** → stop. The roster\'s \\"No booking pass\\" section lists\\r\\n  these. Booking access has to be granted before there is anything to send.\\r\\n- **Pass `exhausted`** → stop, and say so. The link is live but has no credits\\r\\n  left, so the student lands on \\"you\'ve used all your sessions\\". Sending it is\\r\\n  worse than sending nothing. Credits have to be added first.\\r\\n- **The URL slug is not the folder slug.** `yahunatan-zetvy` is\\r\\n  `/book/yahunathan`. Always read it from the roster; never derive it.\\r\\n- **Email disagrees with the backend** → stop and ask which is current. The\\r\\n  roster surfaces these rather than picking one.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe roster\'s booking columns are read **live** from `booking_passes` on every\\r\\nrebuild, so they are current as of the rebuild and revoked passes are already\\r\\nexcluded. That is why step 1 rebuilds first.\\r\\n\\r\\n## 2. Draft in Joshua\'s voice\\r\\n\\r\\nRoute through `wiki/teaching-voice.md`. This is student-facing copy, so the\\r\\nvoice rules are not optional.\\r\\n\\r\\nShape: short, warm, no overselling. Own any delay in the first line if there\\r\\nhas been one, give the real reason in a clause, move to the next step. Hand\\r\\nthem the link plainly. No em-dashes. No AI-slop vocabulary.\\r\\n\\r\\nPersonalize from the student\'s folder — `teaching-notes.md`, `open-loops.md`,\\r\\ntheir `<slug>.md` — so the email refers to where they actually are (what they\\r\\nwere last working on, what they said they wanted). A generic blast is the thing\\r\\nthis skill exists to avoid.\\r\\n\\r\\n## 3. Draft, then stop\\r\\n\\r\\n**Default is draft, not send.** Anything a student or prospect reads is drafted\\r\\nand never sent unless it is a pre-approved template and Joshua has said go.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe safety flag is `--draft`. It is the difference between a draft and a sent\\r\\nemail, so it is never omitted on the first pass.\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\ngws gmail +send --to <email> --subject \\"<subject>\\" --body \\"<text>\\" --draft\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nShow Joshua the drafted text. Send only after an explicit go-ahead, and only\\r\\nfor the students he named — the same command with `--draft` removed:\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\ngws gmail +send --to <email> --subject \\"<subject>\\" --body \\"<text>\\"\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nUse `--dry-run` first if you are unsure the command is well-formed. Note\\r\\n`--body` takes the text inline, not a file path.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor a batch, draft **all** of them and present the set for one approval, rather\\r\\nthan asking per student. Never send a batch on a single \\"yes\\" unless he says\\r\\n\\"send them all\\" plainly.\\r\\n\\r\\n## 4. Log the loop\\r\\n\\r\\nAppend to `students/<slug>/open-loops.md`, matching the existing format:\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\n- [YYYY-MM-DD] Sent booking-link email (/book/<slug>). Loop: confirm they schedule; follow up if no booking within ~5 days.\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nUse the real date (`date +%F`). If it was drafted but not sent, say `Drafted`\\r\\nrather than `Sent` — a wrong entry there is worse than no entry.\\r\\n\\r\\n`open-loops.md` is a **primary** file: append, never rewrite.\\r\\n\\r\\nThen append one line to `wiki/send-ledger.md`, which is the single surface that\\r\\nanswers \\"did X get their email\\":\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\n| YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM | <slug> | booking link (/book/<slug>) | drafted | — |\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nStatus becomes `sent` only when it actually goes out. The per-student log\\r\\ncarries the follow-up loop; the ledger carries whether it was sent.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Hard rules\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Never send without an explicit go-ahead.** Draft is the default, always.\\r\\n- **Never invent an email address or a booking slug.** Missing data stops the\\r\\n  run; it does not get filled in with a guess.\\r\\n- **Never write to `*.generated.md`.** The roster is rebuilt, not edited.\\r\\n- **Log what actually happened.** Drafted is not Sent. If a send fails, log the\\r\\n  failure rather than the intent.\\r\\n- One student\'s email never mentions another student.\\r\\n- If Joshua asks \\"who still needs a booking link\\", answer from the roster\'s\\r\\n  gap sections — that is what they are for — and do not draft anything until\\r\\n  he picks.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n### skills\\\\claude\\\\setup-matt-pocock-skills\\\\SKILL.md\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: setup-matt-pocock-skills\\r\\ndescription: \\"Configure this repo for the engineering skills: set up its issue tracker, triage label vocabulary, and domain doc layout. Run once before first use of the other engineering skills.\\"\\r\\ndisable-model-invocation: true\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Setup Matt Pocock\'s Skills\\r\\n\\r\\nScaffold the per-repo configuration that the engineering skills assume:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Issue tracker**: where issues live (GitHub by default; local markdown is also supported out of the box)\\r\\n- **Triage labels**: the strings used for the five canonical triage roles\\r\\n- **Domain docs**: where `GLOSSARY.md` and ADRs live, and the consumer rules for reading them\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is a prompt-driven skill, not a deterministic script. Explore, present what you found, confirm with the user, then write.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Process\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1. Explore\\r\\n\\r\\nLook at the current repo to understand its starting state. Read whatever exists; don\'t assume:\\r\\n\\r\\n- `git remote -v` and `.git/config`: is this a GitHub repo? Which one?\\r\\n- `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` at the repo root: does either exist? Is there already an `## Agent skills` section in either?\\r\\n- `GLOSSARY.md` and `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` at the repo root\\r\\n- `docs/adr/` and any `src/*/docs/adr/` directories\\r\\n- `docs/agents/`: does this skill\'s prior output already exist?\\r\\n- `.scratch/`: a sign that a local-markdown issue tracker convention is already in use\\r\\n- Is the `triage` skill installed? (a `triage` skill folder alongside this one, or `triage` in your available skills.) This decides whether Section B runs at all.\\r\\n- Monorepo signals: a `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, a `workspaces` field in `package.json`, or a populated `packages/*` with its own `src/`. These are present only in a genuinely large multi-package repo; their absence means single-context, which is almost every repo.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2. Present findings and ask\\r\\n\\r\\nSummarise what\'s present and what\'s missing. Then take the sections in order. One section, one answer, then the next.\\r\\n\\r\\nLead each section with the recommended answer so the user can accept it in a word. Give a one-line explainer only when the choice genuinely branches; skip the section entirely when exploration already settled it (Section B when `triage` isn\'t installed, Section C when there\'s no monorepo).\\r\\n\\r\\n**Section A: Issue tracker.**\\r\\n\\r\\n> Explainer: The \\"issue tracker\\" is where issues live for this repo. Skills like `to-tickets`, `triage`, and `to-spec` read from and write to it. They need to know whether to call `gh issue create`, write a markdown file under `.scratch/`, or follow some other workflow you describe. Pick the place you actually track work for this repo.\\r\\n\\r\\nDefault posture: these skills were designed for GitHub. If a `git remote` points at GitHub, propose that. If a `git remote` points at GitLab (`gitlab.com` or a self-hosted host), propose GitLab. Otherwise (or if the user prefers), offer:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **GitHub**: issues live in the repo\'s GitHub Issues (uses the `gh` CLI)\\r\\n- **GitLab**: issues live in the repo\'s GitLab Issues (uses the [`glab`](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/cli) CLI)\\r\\n- **Local markdown**: issues live as files under `.scratch/<feature>/` in this repo (good for solo projects or repos without a remote)\\r\\n- **Other** (Jira, Linear, etc.): ask the user to describe the workflow in one paragraph; the skill will record it as freeform prose\\r\\n\\r\\nRecord the choice in `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`. The GitHub and GitLab templates carry a \\"PRs as a request surface\\" flag, defaulted **off**. Leave it off and don\'t raise it: a user who wants external PRs in the triage queue can flip the flag in the file later.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Section B: Triage label vocabulary.** Skip this section entirely if the `triage` skill isn\'t installed (exploration told you), since an uninstalled skill needs no labels.\\r\\n\\r\\nIf it is installed, ask exactly one question:\\r\\n\\r\\n> Do you want to keep the default triage labels? (recommended: **yes**)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe defaults are the five canonical roles, each label string equal to its name: `needs-triage`, `needs-info`, `ready-for-agent`, `ready-for-human`, `wontfix`. On **yes**, write them as-is. Only if the user says no, usually because their tracker already uses other names (e.g. `bug:triage` for `needs-triage`), collect the overrides so `triage` applies existing labels instead of creating duplicates.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Section C: Domain docs.** Default to **single-context** (one `GLOSSARY.md` + `docs/adr/` at the repo root). This fits almost every repo; write it without asking.\\r\\n\\r\\nOffer **multi-context** (a root `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` pointing to per-context `GLOSSARY.md` files) only when exploration found monorepo signals. Then confirm which layout they want.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 3. Confirm and edit\\r\\n\\r\\nShow the user a draft of:\\r\\n\\r\\n- The `## Agent skills` block to add to whichever of `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` is being edited (see step 4 for selection rules)\\r\\n- The contents of `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`, `docs/agents/domain.md`, and `docs/agents/triage-labels.md` (the last only when `triage` is installed)\\r\\n\\r\\nLet them edit before writing.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 4. Write\\r\\n\\r\\n**Pick the file to edit:**\\r\\n\\r\\n- If `CLAUDE.md` exists, edit it.\\r\\n- Else if `AGENTS.md` exists, edit it.\\r\\n- If neither exists, ask the user which one to create; don\'t pick for them.\\r\\n\\r\\nNever create `AGENTS.md` when `CLAUDE.md` already exists (or vice versa); always edit the one that\'s already there.\\r\\n\\r\\nIf an `## Agent skills` block already exists in the chosen file, update its contents in-place rather than appending a duplicate. Don\'t overwrite user edits to the surrounding sections.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe block:\\r\\n\\r\\n```markdown\\r\\n## Agent skills\\r\\n\\r\\n### Issue tracker\\r\\n\\r\\n[one-line summary of where issues are tracked]. See `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Triage labels\\r\\n\\r\\n[one-line summary of the label vocabulary]. See `docs/agents/triage-labels.md`.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Domain docs\\r\\n\\r\\n[one-line summary of layout: \\"single-context\\" or \\"multi-context\\"]. See `docs/agents/domain.md`.\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nInclude the `### Triage labels` sub-block, and write `docs/agents/triage-labels.md`, only when `triage` is installed and Section B ran. When it isn\'t, both are omitted.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen Section B ran on GitHub or GitLab, create each configured label the tracker lacks (`gh label create` / `glab label create`).\\r\\n\\r\\nThen write the docs files using the seed templates in this skill folder as a starting point:\\r\\n\\r\\n- [issue-tracker-github.md](./issue-tracker-github.md): GitHub issue tracker\\r\\n- [issue-tracker-gitlab.md](./issue-tracker-gitlab.md): GitLab issue tracker\\r\\n- [issue-tracker-local.md](./issue-tracker-local.md): local-markdown issue tracker\\r\\n- [triage-labels.md](./triage-labels.md): label mapping (only if `triage` is installed)\\r\\n- [domain.md](./domain.md): domain doc consumer rules + layout\\r\\n\\r\\nFor \\"other\\" issue trackers, write `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md` from scratch using the user\'s description.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 5. Done\\r\\n\\r\\nTell the user the setup is complete and which engineering skills will now read from these files. Mention they can edit `docs/agents/*.md` directly later; re-running this skill is only necessary if they want to switch issue trackers or restart from scratch.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n### skills\\\\claude\\\\setup-pre-commit\\\\SKILL.md\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: setup-pre-commit\\r\\ndescription: Set up Husky pre-commit hooks with lint-staged (Prettier), type checking, and tests in the current repo. Use when user wants to add pre-commit hooks, set up Husky, configure lint-staged, or add commit-time formatting/typechecking/testing.\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Setup Pre-Commit Hooks\\r\\n\\r\\n## What This Sets Up\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Husky** pre-commit hook\\r\\n- **lint-staged** running Prettier on all staged files\\r\\n- **Prettier** config (if missing)\\r\\n- **typecheck** and **test** scripts in the pre-commit hook\\r\\n\\r\\n## Steps\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1. Detect package manager\\r\\n\\r\\nCheck for `package-lock.json` (npm), `pnpm-lock.yaml` (pnpm), `yarn.lock` (yarn), `bun.lockb` (bun). Use whichever is present. Default to npm if unclear.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2. Install dependencies\\r\\n\\r\\nInstall as devDependencies:\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\nhusky lint-staged prettier\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n### 3. Initialize Husky\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\nnpx husky init\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThis creates `.husky/` dir and adds `prepare: \\"husky\\"` to package.json.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 4. Create `.husky/pre-commit`\\r\\n\\r\\nWrite this file (no shebang needed for Husky v9+):\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\nnpx lint-staged\\r\\nnpm run typecheck\\r\\nnpm run test\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**Adapt**: Replace `npm` with detected package manager. If repo has no `typecheck` or `test` script in package.json, omit those lines and tell the user.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 5. Create `.lintstagedrc`\\r\\n\\r\\n```json\\r\\n{\\r\\n  \\"*\\": \\"prettier --ignore-unknown --write\\"\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n### 6. Create `.prettierrc` (if missing)\\r\\n\\r\\nOnly create if no Prettier config exists. Use these defaults:\\r\\n\\r\\n```json\\r\\n{\\r\\n  \\"useTabs\\": false,\\r\\n  \\"tabWidth\\": 2,\\r\\n  \\"printWidth\\": 80,\\r\\n  \\"singleQuote\\": false,\\r\\n  \\"trailingComma\\": \\"es5\\",\\r\\n  \\"semi\\": true,\\r\\n  \\"arrowParens\\": \\"always\\"\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n### 7. Verify\\r\\n\\r\\n- [ ] `.husky/pre-commit` exists and is executable\\r\\n- [ ] `.lintstagedrc` exists\\r\\n- [ ] `prepare` script in package.json is `\\"husky\\"`\\r\\n- [ ] `prettier` config exists\\r\\n- [ ] Run `npx lint-staged` to verify it works\\r\\n\\r\\n### 8. Commit\\r\\n\\r\\nStage all changed/created files and commit with message: `Add pre-commit hooks (husky + lint-staged + prettier)`\\r\\n\\r\\nThis will run through the new pre-commit hooks: a good smoke test that everything works.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Notes\\r\\n\\r\\n- Husky v9+ doesn\'t need shebangs in hook files\\r\\n- `prettier --ignore-unknown` skips files Prettier can\'t parse (images, etc.)\\r\\n- The pre-commit runs lint-staged first (fast, staged-only), then full typecheck and tests\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n### skills\\\\claude\\\\setup-ts-deep-modules\\\\SKILL.md\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: setup-ts-deep-modules\\r\\ndescription: Wire dependency-cruiser into a TypeScript repo so each package is a deep module, with implementation hidden in subfolders and reachable only through its entry-point files. User-invoked.\\r\\ndisable-model-invocation: true\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Setup TS Deep Modules\\r\\n\\r\\nMake every package in this repo a **deep module**: a lot of behaviour behind a small interface. A package\'s public surface is its **entry points** (the files at the package root), and everything in its subfolders is hidden. This skill installs [dependency-cruiser](https://github.com/sverweij/dependency-cruiser) and the rules that make the entry points the only way in, then proves the rules bite.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor the vocabulary (deep module, interface, seam, depth), call the Skill tool with \\"codebase-design\\" and use its language throughout.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The shape this enforces\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\nsrc/packages/\\r\\n  <name>/\\r\\n    index.ts        ← an entry point (public). Import this from outside.\\r\\n    client.ts       ← another entry point. Packages may expose SEVERAL.\\r\\n    lib/            ← implementation: hidden from outside, free to import each other.\\r\\n    tests/          ← co-located tests + fixtures (a subfolder, so private).\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThe public surface is the package\'s **root files**, not one designated `index.ts`. By convention implementation lives in `lib/` and tests in `tests/`, giving every package the same two-folder shape. The rule itself is general, though: *anything* in *any* subfolder is private, so you never extend the config to add a folder.\\r\\n\\r\\nFour rules, all `error`:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Entry-point boundary**: code outside a package (app code or another package) may import only that package\'s entry points (its root files), never anything in its subfolders.\\r\\n2. **Intra-package freedom**: a package\'s own files import each other freely.\\r\\n3. **Tests through the entry points**: files under `<pkg>/tests/` may import any package\'s entry points and their own `tests/` fixtures, but never any package\'s subfolder internals (not even their own). Integration tests across packages are fine; deep imports are not.\\r\\n4. **No cycles**: no dependency cycles.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Entry points, not a barrel.** Because the public surface is *every* root file, a package can expose several small entry points (`index.ts`, `client.ts`, `server.ts`) instead of funnelling everything through one giant `index.ts`. Barrel files that re-export a whole subtree are discouraged; keep entry points small and hide implementation in subfolders.\\r\\n\\r\\nLayering (which packages may depend on which) is a *different* concern and is left as a commented stub in the config for this repo to fill in.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Steps\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1. Detect the environment\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Package manager**: `pnpm-lock.yaml` → pnpm, `yarn.lock` → yarn, `bun.lockb` → bun, else npm. Use it for every command below (`pnpm`/`yarn`/`npm run`/`bunx`).\\r\\n- **Packages root**: if `src/` exists use `src/packages`, else `packages`. Confirm the choice with the user if the repo already has a different obvious convention.\\r\\n- **Existing config**: check for a `.dependency-cruiser.*` file. If one exists, do **not** overwrite it: merge the four rules and the options in, and tell the user what you added.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Done when:** package manager, packages root, and existing-config status are all known.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2. Install dependency-cruiser\\r\\n\\r\\nInstall `dependency-cruiser` as a devDependency with the detected package manager.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Done when:** `dependency-cruiser` is in `devDependencies`.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 3. Write the config\\r\\n\\r\\nCopy [`dependency-cruiser.config.cjs`](./dependency-cruiser.config.cjs) to the repo root as `.dependency-cruiser.cjs`. Set `PACKAGES_ROOT` to the root detected in step 1. The rules are path-depth based and extension-agnostic, so nothing else needs adapting.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Done when:** `.dependency-cruiser.cjs` exists with the correct `PACKAGES_ROOT`, and the four forbidden rules are present.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 4. Wire it into the checks\\r\\n\\r\\n- Add a `lint:boundaries` script: `depcruise <packages-root>` (or `depcruise src`).\\r\\n- Fold it into the repo\'s umbrella check command, the one that already runs typecheck (e.g. a `check` / `ci` / `validate` script). Do **not** touch `tsconfig` or add path aliases.\\r\\n- If there is no umbrella script, add `lint:boundaries` and tell the user to include it in CI.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Done when:** `lint:boundaries` exists and runs as part of the same command as typecheck.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 5. Scaffold the example package\\r\\n\\r\\nCreate a committed `<packages-root>/example/` as a copy-me template:\\r\\n\\r\\n- `index.ts` is an entry point. Export one function that delegates to an internal file (so the package is visibly *deep*, not a pass-through).\\r\\n- `lib/impl.ts`: an internal file in a **subfolder**, imported by `index.ts`, not reachable from outside.\\r\\n- `tests/example.test.ts` imports **only** `../index` (an entry point) and asserts against the public function.\\r\\n\\r\\nTell the user this is a starter template to copy or delete.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Done when:** the example package exists, exposes its behaviour through a root entry point, and hides `impl` in a subfolder.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 6. Prove the rules bite\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is the completion criterion for the whole skill: a config that doesn\'t fail on a violation is worthless.\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Run `lint:boundaries`. It must **pass** on the clean example.\\r\\n2. Temporarily add a deep import to `tests/example.test.ts` (e.g. `import { thing } from \\"../lib/impl\\"`). Run `lint:boundaries` again; it must **fail** with `tests-through-entrypoints`.\\r\\n3. Revert the deep import. Run once more, and it must **pass**.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Done when:** you have observed a pass, then a fail on the deep import, then a pass again. If step 2 does not fail, the rules are not wired correctly, so fix before finishing.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 7. Document the convention\\r\\n\\r\\nWrite a `README.md` **in the packages folder** (`<packages-root>/README.md`, next to the packages it governs) covering: the `src/packages/<name>/` layout (entry points at the root, `lib/` for implementation, `tests/` for tests), \\"import only through a package\'s entry points (its root files)\\", and how to run `lint:boundaries`. **Discourage barrel files** explicitly: expose several small entry points instead of re-exporting a whole subtree through one index. Keep it to the copy-me snippet plus the four rules in one paragraph each.\\r\\n\\r\\nThen add a **context pointer** to it from the repo\'s agent-instructions file (`CLAUDE.md` if present, else `AGENTS.md`, creating `AGENTS.md` if neither exists). One line is enough, e.g. `Packages are deep modules: see [src/packages/README.md](./src/packages/README.md) before adding or importing one.` This is what makes an agent discover the boundary rule instead of tripping over it.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Done when:** `<packages-root>/README.md` exists and discourages barrels, and the repo\'s `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` links to it.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Notes\\r\\n\\r\\n- The config\'s `$1` back-references (dependency-cruiser\'s group matching) are what let a package reach its own internals while outsiders can\'t. Don\'t flatten them into separate per-package rules.\\r\\n- Public vs private is decided by **depth**: a package\'s root files are entry points; anything in a subfolder is private. The conventional subfolders are `lib/` (implementation) and `tests/`, but the rule doesn\'t hardcode them: any subfolder is private, so a new folder never needs a config change. Adding an entry point is just adding a root file (no barrel).\\r\\n- Packages are **flat**: one tier of immediate children under the root. A package\'s internals may nest as deep as you like; a package may not contain another package.\\r\\n- Use `.cjs` (not `.js`) so the config\'s `module.exports` works even in `\\"type\\": \\"module\\"` repos.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n### skills\\\\claude\\\\superwhisper\\\\SKILL.md\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: superwhisper\\r\\ndescription: \\"Use whenever Joshua wants anything changed in Superwhisper, his dictation app on the Windows laptop. Triggers on \\\\\\"save X in my vocabulary\\\\\\", \\\\\\"add X to my dictionary\\\\\\", \\\\\\"X --> Y\\\\\\", \\\\\\"X should always be Y\\\\\\", \\\\\\"replace X with Y\\\\\\", a bare mis-heard word with an arrow, \\\\\\"make a mode for ...\\\\\\", \\\\\\"scan my transcripts\\\\\\", \\\\\\"what keeps getting messed up\\\\\\", \\\\\\"what should I add to Superwhisper\\\\\\", \\\\\\"restart Superwhisper\\\\\\", and any mention of Superwhisper, Super Whisper, or \\\\\\"the dictation\\\\\\" in the same breath as a word, a spelling, or a mode. Also use it when a dictated message from Joshua arrives with an obvious mis-hearing of a known term, even if he does not ask: note it and offer the fix. Covers the whole loop: edit the vault files, think through the likely mis-hearing variants, sync into the app, restart it silently, verify the load, and scan the transcript history for the next improvements.\\"\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Superwhisper\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua dictates almost everything he sends you. Superwhisper is the app that does it, and the\\r\\n`dev/ai-os/superwhisper/` folder is its source of truth. Your job is to keep that folder right\\r\\nand get it into the app without him having to touch anything. He uses Left Alt to toggle recording; preserve it and verify it after restart.\\r\\n\\r\\nRead `dev/ai-os/superwhisper/CLAUDE.md` first if this is a new session. It holds the rules\\r\\nthat cost a whole session to learn (the Claude Desktop sandbox redirects writes, the app\\r\\nreads config only at launch, prompt examples cannot be written from outside the app). This\\r\\nskill assumes those rules; it does not repeat them.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The three requests\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1. A word or a correction (\\"Firecrow --> Firecrawl\\", \\"save Pre-workout\\")\\r\\n\\r\\nDecide which of two files it belongs in. They do different jobs:\\r\\n\\r\\n- `replacements.md` fixes a specific mis-hearing. Deterministic, case-insensitive, applied\\r\\n  after transcription. This is where almost everything goes.\\r\\n- `vocabulary.md` is a hint list sent to the voice model. Keep it around 40 entries: names and\\r\\n  terms the model cannot know. On 2026-09-11 it was pushed to 654 (every replacement target\\r\\n  auto-added) and transcription got noticeably worse within the hour, so that rule is gone;\\r\\n  the sync sends exactly the listed terms. Add a vocabulary line only for a term the model\\r\\n  keeps getting wrong.\\r\\n\\r\\nA correction with an arrow is a replacement row only. \\"Save the word X\\" means a vocabulary\\r\\nline (if the model really cannot know it) plus replacement rows for how it gets mangled.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Think through the variants before writing.** One row per spelling he sends is not enough;\\r\\nhe sends the next mis-hearing ten minutes later. For each term, write rows for:\\r\\n\\r\\n- the exact form he sent, lowercase on the heard side\\r\\n- the same with a trailing period (`firecrow.`), because a one-word dictation gets\\r\\n  auto-punctuated and the rule will not match with the period attached\\r\\n- phonetic neighbours: swapped vowels (fisseha → faseya, fuseya, fasaya, fesaya), doubled\\r\\n  or dropped letters (firecrawll, firecraw), split or joined words (pre workout, preworkout,\\r\\n  cloudcode)\\r\\n- spoken forms of anything with punctuation: \\"at ... dot com\\", \\"dot study\\"\\r\\n- a casing pin when the wanted form has specific casing (`pre-workout` → `Pre-workout`,\\r\\n  `lsatprep.study` lowercase, `LSATU` → `LSAT U`)\\r\\n- the bare surname or bare product name, not only the full email or phrase\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not add a row whose heard side is an ordinary English word or number (\\"seven\\" → Steven,\\r\\n\\"white\\" → Whit, \\"care\\" → Charles, \\"and review\\" → blind review). It would fire inside normal\\r\\nsentences. When a scan suggests one of those, say so and leave it out.\\r\\n\\r\\nNote the trade-off on trailing-period rows: a sentence that genuinely ends with the word\\r\\nloses its full stop. Say this once when you add the first such row; do not repeat it.\\r\\n\\r\\nThen run the loop (below). The whole thing is one turn: he sends the word, you reply with\\r\\nwhat you added and the loaded counts. No questions unless the target spelling is ambiguous.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2. A mode (\\"make a mode for ...\\")\\r\\n\\r\\nCopy the closest file in `modes/` to a new `modes/<key>.md`. Frontmatter is the config\\r\\n(key, name, type, voice_model `sv-1`, language_model, the three context flags, auto_paste);\\r\\nthe body is the prompt; `## Examples` with `### Input` / `### Output` pairs are appended to\\r\\nthe prompt text by the sync (the app rejects examples written any other way).\\r\\n\\r\\nWhat makes his prompts work, from the docs and the community collections in\\r\\n`superwhisper/research/`:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Name the inputs exactly: User Message, Application Context, Selected Text, Clipboard\\r\\n  Context. Say the User Message is dictated speech.\\r\\n- Any mode whose output goes to an AI agent needs the \\"you are not an assistant\\" block with\\r\\n  WRONG/CORRECT pairs, or the model answers the dictation instead of cleaning it. Copy it\\r\\n  from `modes/claude-code.md`.\\r\\n- Anything student-facing routes through `wiki/teaching-voice.md`: no em dashes, no hype\\r\\n  words, short lines, \\"Hi [Name],\\" / \\"Best, Joshua\\".\\r\\n- Turn on only the context the mode needs. Selection is captured at record start, clipboard\\r\\n  within 3 s before or during, application after transcription.\\r\\n- Language model: Joshua chose S1-Language (`sl-1`) for all modes on 2026-09-11 for speed.\\r\\n  Keep that unless he asks; `sw-claude-4p5-sonnet` is the confirmed upgrade if a mode needs\\r\\n  judgment.\\r\\n\\r\\nThen run the loop. Add the mode to the table in `superwhisper/CLAUDE.md`.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 3. A scan (\\"what keeps going wrong\\", \\"scan my transcripts\\", or every week or so unprompted)\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\npython C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/superwhisper/scan.py            # all history\\r\\npython C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/superwhisper/scan.py --since 7  # last week\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nIt reads every recording\'s raw transcript and writes `research/SCAN-<date>.md` with four\\r\\nsections: near-misses of known terms (these become replacement rows), replacement rules\\r\\nthat did not fire after their date (means the app was not restarted, or the spelling\\r\\ndiffers), candidate terms seen often with varying spellings (worth adding), and the most\\r\\nused domain words.\\r\\n\\r\\nTurn the report into a short offer, not a dump: the rows you would add (and why), the ones\\r\\nyou are deliberately skipping (and why), and any mode-level improvement the transcripts\\r\\nsuggest (for example, if most of the week\'s dictations were instructions to an agent and\\r\\nthe Claude Code mode is not the active one, say so). Apply the safe rows in the same turn,\\r\\nrun the loop, and leave the judgment calls to him.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The loop\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery change ends the same way. `sync.py --restart` does all of it:\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\npython C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/superwhisper/sync.py --restart\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Reads `vocabulary.md`, `replacements.md`, `modes/*.md`.\\r\\n2. Backs up the app\'s `settings.json`, then writes vocabulary, replacements, modeKeys, and\\r\\n   every mode file through the `\\\\\\\\localhost\\\\C$` path (the sandbox bypass).\\r\\n3. Quits Superwhisper and relaunches it through Task Scheduler so it runs outside the\\r\\n   sandbox, silently, in the background. Nothing appears on his screen; he keeps using\\r\\n   Left Alt.\\r\\n4. Reads `modeKeys` back. The app rewrites that list at launch and drops any mode it\\r\\n   rejected, so this is the only proof that a change loaded. A write is not a load.\\r\\n\\r\\nReport the last line it prints (replacements / vocabulary / modes loaded). If the mode\\r\\ncount is lower than the number of files in `modes/`, a mode was rejected: diff the loaded\\r\\nlist against the files and fix before saying done.\\r\\n\\r\\n`python sync.py --check` shows the diff without writing, for when you want to confirm\\r\\nbefore touching anything.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Things not to do\\r\\n\\r\\n- Do not open the Settings window, the app, or anything visible after a restart. He asked\\r\\n  for this explicitly on 2026-09-11. If he needs Settings, `superwhisper://settings` or the\\r\\n  \\"Superwhisper Settings\\" shortcut on his Desktop opens it.\\r\\n- Do not launch `Superwhisper.exe` with Start-Process from this shell. It starts a\\r\\n  sandboxed second copy whose tray icon does not work. Only the scheduler route in\\r\\n  `sync.py`.\\r\\n- Do not edit the app\'s JSON by hand. Edit the vault files; the sync owns the JSON.\\r\\n- Do not pad the vocabulary. When in doubt, it is a replacement.\\r\\n- Do not batch his corrections for later. Each one lands, syncs, restarts, and is reported in\\r\\n  the turn it arrives, even mid-task.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Files\\r\\n\\r\\n| Path | Role |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| `dev/ai-os/superwhisper/CLAUDE.md` | The rules. Read first. |\\r\\n| `dev/ai-os/superwhisper/vocabulary.md`, `replacements.md` | The lists. Edit these. |\\r\\n| `dev/ai-os/superwhisper/modes/*.md` | One file per mode. |\\r\\n| `dev/ai-os/superwhisper/sync.py` | Push + restart + verify. |\\r\\n| `dev/ai-os/superwhisper/scan.py` | Transcript scan → `research/SCAN-<date>.md`. |\\r\\n| `dev/ai-os/superwhisper/research/` | The 2026-09-11 customization report, sources, scans. |\\r\\n| `wiki/SUPERWHISPER-DICTIONARY.md` | Dated history ledger; append a line when something notable changes. |\\r\\n\\r\\n"}'}]

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 17.3 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"a92f07","wall_time_seconds":2.228827,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":6426,"output":"\\r\\n### skills\\\\claude\\\\teach\\\\SKILL.md\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: teach\\r\\ndescription: Teach the user a new skill or concept, within this workspace.\\r\\ndisable-model-invocation: true\\r\\nargument-hint: \\"What would you like to learn about?\\"\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\nThe user has asked you to teach them something. This is a stateful request - they intend to learn the topic over multiple sessions.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Teaching Workspace\\r\\n\\r\\nTreat the current directory as a teaching workspace. Workspace paths (`./lessons/` and the rest) resolve from the directory `/teach` was run in; only the `*-FORMAT.md` links resolve from this skill\'s folder. The state of their learning is captured in this directory in several files:\\r\\n\\r\\n- `MISSION.md`: A document capturing the _reason_ the user is interested in the topic. This should be used to ground all teaching. Use the format in [MISSION-FORMAT.md](./MISSION-FORMAT.md).\\r\\n- `./reference/*.html`: A directory of reference materials. These are the compressed learnings from the lessons - cheat sheets, reference algorithms, syntax, yoga poses, glossaries. They are the raw units of learning. They should be beautiful documents which print out well, and are designed for quick reference.\\r\\n- `RESOURCES.md`: A list of resources which can be explored to ground your teaching in contextual knowledge, or to acquire knowledge and wisdom. Use the format in [RESOURCES-FORMAT.md](./RESOURCES-FORMAT.md).\\r\\n- `./learning-records/*.md`: A directory of learning records, which capture what the user has learned. These are loosely equivalent to architectural decision records in software development - they capture non-obvious lessons and key insights that may need to be revised later, or drive future sessions. These should be used to calculate the zone of proximal development. They are titled `0001-<dash-case-name>.md`, where the number increments each time. Use the format in [LEARNING-RECORD-FORMAT.md](./LEARNING-RECORD-FORMAT.md).\\r\\n- `./lessons/*.html`: A directory of lessons. A **lesson** is a single, self-contained HTML output that teaches one tightly-scoped thing tied to the mission. This is the primary unit of teaching in this workspace.\\r\\n- `./assets/*`: Reusable **components** shared across lessons. See [Assets](#assets).\\r\\n- `NOTES.md`: A scratchpad for you to jot down user preferences, or working notes.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Philosophy\\r\\n\\r\\nTo learn at a deep level, the user needs three things:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Knowledge**, captured from high-quality, high-trust resources\\r\\n- **Skills**, acquired through highly-relevant interactive lessons devised by you, based on the knowledge\\r\\n- **Wisdom**, which comes from interacting with other learners and practitioners\\r\\n\\r\\nBefore the `RESOURCES.md` is well-populated, your focus should be to find high-quality resources which will help the user acquire knowledge. Never trust your parametric knowledge.\\r\\n\\r\\nSome topics may require more skills than knowledge. Learning more about theoretical physics might be more knowledge-based. For yoga, more skills-based.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Fluency vs Storage Strength\\r\\n\\r\\nYou should be careful to split between two types of learning:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Fluency strength**: in-the-moment retrieval of knowledge\\r\\n- **Storage strength**: long-term retention of knowledge\\r\\n\\r\\nFluency can give the user an illusory sense of mastery, but storage strength is the real goal. Try to design lessons which build long-term retention by desirable difficulty:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Using retrieval practice (recall from memory)\\r\\n- Spacing (distributing practice over time)\\r\\n- Interleaving (mixing up different but related topics in practice - for skills practice only)\\r\\n\\r\\n## Lessons\\r\\n\\r\\nA lesson is the main thing you produce: the unit in which knowledge and skills reach the user. Each lesson is one self-contained HTML file, saved to `./lessons/` and titled `0001-<dash-case-name>.html` where the number increments each time.\\r\\n\\r\\nA lesson should be **beautiful**, with clean, readable typography and layout, since the user will return to these later to review. Think Tufte.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe lesson should be short, and completable very quickly. Learners\' working memory is very small, and we need to stay within it. But each lesson should give the user a single tangible win that they can build on. It should be directly tied to the mission, and should be in the user\'s zone of proximal development.\\r\\n\\r\\nIf possible, open the lesson file for the user by running a CLI command.\\r\\n\\r\\nEach lesson should link via HTML anchors to other lessons and reference documents.\\r\\n\\r\\nEach lesson should recommend a primary source for the user to read or watch. This should be the most high-quality, high-trust resource you found on the topic.\\r\\n\\r\\nEach lesson should contain a reminder to ask followup questions to the agent. The agent is their teacher, and can assist with anything that\'s unclear.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Assets\\r\\n\\r\\nLessons are built from reusable **components**, stored in `./assets/`: stylesheets, quiz widgets, simulators, diagram helpers, and anything else a second lesson could reuse.\\r\\n\\r\\nReuse is the default, not the exception. Before authoring a lesson, read `./assets/` and build from the components already there. When a lesson needs something new and reusable, write it as a component in `./assets/` and link to it; never inline code a future lesson would duplicate.\\r\\n\\r\\nA shared stylesheet is the first component every workspace earns: every lesson links it, so the lessons look like one consistent course rather than a pile of one-offs. As the workspace grows, so should the component library.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The Mission\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery lesson should be tied into the mission - the reason that the user is interested in learning about the topic.\\r\\n\\r\\nIf the user is unclear about the mission, or the `MISSION.md` is not populated, your first job should be to question the user on why they want to learn this.\\r\\n\\r\\nFailing to understand the mission will mean knowledge acquisition is not grounded in real-world goals. Lessons will feel too abstract. You will have no way of judging what the user should do next.\\r\\n\\r\\nMissions may change as the user develops more skills and knowledge. This is normal - make sure to update the `MISSION.md` and add a learning record to capture the change. Confirm with the user before changing the mission.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Zone Of Proximal Development\\r\\n\\r\\nEach lesson, the user should always feel as if they are being challenged \'just enough\'.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe user may specify an exact thing they want to learn. If they don\'t, figure out their zone of proximal development by:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Reading their `learning-records`\\r\\n- Figuring out the right thing to teach them based on their mission\\r\\n- Teach the most relevant thing that fits in their zone of proximal development\\r\\n\\r\\n## Knowledge\\r\\n\\r\\nLessons should be designed around a skill the user is going to learn. The knowledge in the lesson should be only what\'s required to acquire that skill. You teach the knowledge first, then get the user to practice the skills via an interactive feedback loop.\\r\\n\\r\\nKnowledge should first be gathered from trusted resources. Use `RESOURCES.md` to keep track of them. Lessons should be littered with citations - links to external resources to back up any claim made. This increases the trustworthiness of the lesson.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor acquiring knowledge, difficulty is the enemy. It eats working memory you need for understanding.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Skills\\r\\n\\r\\nIf knowledge is all about acquisition, skills are about durability and flexibility. Make the knowledge stick.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor skill acquisition, difficulty is the tool. Effortful retrieval is what builds storage strength. Skills should be taught through interactive lessons. There are several tools at your disposal:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Interactive lessons, using quizzes and light in-browser tasks\\r\\n- Lessons which guide the user through a list of real-world steps to take (for instance, yoga poses)\\r\\n\\r\\nEach of these should be based on a **feedback loop**, where the user receives feedback on their performance. This feedback loop should be as tight as possible, giving feedback immediately - and ideally automatically.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor quizzes, each answer should be exactly the same number of words (and characters, if possible). Vary which position holds the correct answer across questions. Don\'t give the user any clues about the answer through formatting or order.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Acquiring Wisdom\\r\\n\\r\\nWisdom comes from true real-world interaction - testing your skills outside the learning environment.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen the user asks a question that appears to require wisdom, your default posture should be to attempt to answer - but to ultimately delegate to a **community**.\\r\\n\\r\\nA community is a place (online or offline) where the user can test their skills in the real world. This might be a forum, a subreddit, a real-world class (budget permitting) or a local interest group.\\r\\n\\r\\nYou should attempt to find high-reputation communities the user can join. If the user expresses a preference that they don\'t want to join a community, respect it.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Reference Documents\\r\\n\\r\\nWhile creating lessons, you should also create reference documents. Lessons can reference these documents - they are useful for tracking raw units of knowledge useful across lessons.\\r\\n\\r\\nLessons will rarely be revisited later - reference documents will be. They should be the compressed essence of the lesson, in a format designed for quick reference.\\r\\n\\r\\nSome learning topics lend themselves to reference:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Syntax and code snippets for programming\\r\\n- Algorithms and flowcharts for processes\\r\\n- Yoga poses and sequences for yoga\\r\\n- Exercises and routines for fitness\\r\\n- Glossaries for any topic with its own nomenclature\\r\\n\\r\\nGlossaries, in particular, are an essential reference. Once one is created, it should be adhered to in every lesson.\\r\\n\\r\\n## `NOTES.md`\\r\\n\\r\\nThe user will sometimes express preferences of how they want to be taught, or things you should keep in mind. This is the place to record those preferences, so you can refer back to them when designing lessons or working with the user.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n### skills\\\\claude\\\\theme-factory\\\\SKILL.md\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: theme-factory\\r\\ndescription: Toolkit for styling artifacts with a theme. These artifacts can be slides, docs, reportings, HTML landing pages, etc. There are 10 pre-set themes with colors/fonts that you can apply to any artifact that has been creating, or can generate a new theme on-the-fly.\\r\\nlicense: Complete terms in LICENSE.txt\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n# Theme Factory Skill\\r\\n\\r\\nThis skill provides a curated collection of professional font and color themes themes, each with carefully selected color palettes and font pairings. Once a theme is chosen, it can be applied to any artifact.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Purpose\\r\\n\\r\\nTo apply consistent, professional styling to presentation slide decks, use this skill. Each theme includes:\\r\\n- A cohesive color palette with hex codes\\r\\n- Complementary font pairings for headers and body text\\r\\n- A distinct visual identity suitable for different contexts and audiences\\r\\n\\r\\n## Usage Instructions\\r\\n\\r\\nTo apply styling to a slide deck or other artifact:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Show the theme showcase**: Display the `theme-showcase.pdf` file to allow users to see all available themes visually. Do not make any modifications to it; simply show the file for viewing.\\r\\n2. **Ask for their choice**: Ask which theme to apply to the deck\\r\\n3. **Wait for selection**: Get explicit confirmation about the chosen theme\\r\\n4. **Apply the theme**: Once a theme has been chosen, apply the selected theme\'s colors and fonts to the deck/artifact\\r\\n\\r\\n## Themes Available\\r\\n\\r\\nThe following 10 themes are available, each showcased in `theme-showcase.pdf`:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Ocean Depths** - Professional and calming maritime theme\\r\\n2. **Sunset Boulevard** - Warm and vibrant sunset colors\\r\\n3. **Forest Canopy** - Natural and grounded earth tones\\r\\n4. **Modern Minimalist** - Clean and contemporary grayscale\\r\\n5. **Golden Hour** - Rich and warm autumnal palette\\r\\n6. **Arctic Frost** - Cool and crisp winter-inspired theme\\r\\n7. **Desert Rose** - Soft and sophisticated dusty tones\\r\\n8. **Tech Innovation** - Bold and modern tech aesthetic\\r\\n9. **Botanical Garden** - Fresh and organic garden colors\\r\\n10. **Midnight Galaxy** - Dramatic and cosmic deep tones\\r\\n\\r\\n## Theme Details\\r\\n\\r\\nEach theme is defined in the `themes/` directory with complete specifications including:\\r\\n- Cohesive color palette with hex codes\\r\\n- Complementary font pairings for headers and body text\\r\\n- Distinct visual identity suitable for different contexts and audiences\\r\\n\\r\\n## Application Process\\r\\n\\r\\nAfter a preferred theme is selected:\\r\\n1. Read the corresponding theme file from the `themes/` directory\\r\\n2. Apply the specified colors and fonts consistently throughout the deck\\r\\n3. Ensure proper contrast and readability\\r\\n4. Maintain the theme\'s visual identity across all slides\\r\\n\\r\\n## Create your Own Theme\\r\\nTo handle cases where none of the existing themes work for an artifact, create a custom theme. Based on provided inputs, generate a new theme similar to the ones above. Give the theme a similar name describing what the font/color combinations represent. Use any basic description provided to choose appropriate colors/fonts. After generating the theme, show it for review and verification. Following that, apply the theme as described above.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n### skills\\\\claude\\\\to-issues\\\\SKILL.md\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: to-issues\\r\\ndescription: Break a plan, spec, or PRD into independently-grabbable issues on the project issue tracker using tracer-bullet vertical slices.\\r\\ndisable-model-invocation: true\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# To Issues\\r\\n\\r\\nBreak a plan into independently-grabbable issues using vertical slices (tracer bullets).\\r\\n\\r\\nThe issue tracker and triage label vocabulary should have been provided to you — run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` if not.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Process\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1. Gather context\\r\\n\\r\\nWork from whatever is already in the conversation context. If the user passes an issue reference (issue number, URL, or path) as an argument, fetch it from the issue tracker and read its full body and comments.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2. Issue titles and descriptions should use the project\'s domain glossary vocabulary, and respect ADRs in the area you\'re touching.\\r\\n\\r\\nLook for opportunities to prefactor the code to make the implementation easier. \\"Make the change easy, then make the easy change.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n### 3. Each issue is a thin vertical slice that cuts through ALL integration layers end-to-end, NOT a horizontal slice of one layer.\\r\\n\\r\\n<vertical-slice-rules>\\r\\n\\r\\n- Each slice delivers a narrow but COMPLETE path through every layer (schema, API, UI, tests)\\r\\n- A completed slice is demoable or verifiable on its own\\r\\n- Any prefactoring should be done first\\r\\n\\r\\n</vertical-slice-rules>\\r\\n\\r\\n### 4. (too coarse / too fine)\\r\\n- Are the dependency relationships correct?\\r\\n- Should any slices be merged or split further?\\r\\n\\r\\nIterate until the user approves the breakdown.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 5. Publish the issues to the issue tracker\\r\\n\\r\\nFor each approved slice, publish a new issue to the issue tracker. Use the issue body template below. These issues are considered ready for AFK agents, so publish them with the correct triage label unless instructed otherwise.\\r\\n\\r\\nPublish issues in dependency order (blockers first) so you can reference real issue identifiers in the \\"Blocked by\\" field.\\r\\n\\r\\n<issue-template>\\r\\n## Parent\\r\\n\\r\\nA reference to the parent issue on the issue tracker (if the source was an existing issue, otherwise omit this section).\\r\\n\\r\\n## What to build\\r\\n\\r\\nA concise description of this vertical slice. Describe the end-to-end behavior, not layer-by-layer implementation.\\r\\n\\r\\nAvoid specific file paths or code snippets — they go stale fast. Trim to the decision-rich parts — not a working demo, just the important bits.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Acceptance criteria\\r\\n\\r\\n- [ ] Criterion 1\\r\\n- [ ] Criterion 2\\r\\n- [ ] Criterion 3\\r\\n\\r\\n## Blocked by\\r\\n\\r\\n- A reference to the blocking ticket (if any)\\r\\n\\r\\nOr \\"None - can start immediately\\" if no blockers.\\r\\n\\r\\n</issue-template>\\r\\n\\r\\nDo NOT close or modify any parent issue.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n### skills\\\\claude\\\\to-spec\\\\SKILL.md\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: to-spec\\r\\ndescription: \\"Turn the current conversation into a spec and publish it to the project issue tracker: no interview, just synthesis of what you\'ve already discussed.\\"\\r\\ndisable-model-invocation: true\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\nThis skill takes the current conversation context and codebase understanding and produces a spec. Do NOT interview the user; just synthesize what you already know.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe issue tracker and triage label vocabulary should have been provided to you. If not, tell the user to run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills`.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Process\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Explore the repo to understand the current state of the codebase, if you haven\'t already. Use the project\'s domain glossary vocabulary throughout the spec, and respect any ADRs in the area you\'re touching.\\r\\n\\r\\n2. Sketch out the seams at which you\'re going to test the feature. Existing seams should be preferred to new ones. Use the highest seam possible. If new seams are needed, propose them at the highest point you can. The fewer seams across the codebase, the better - the ideal number is one.\\r\\n\\r\\nCheck with the user that these seams match their expectations.\\r\\n\\r\\n3. Write the spec using the template below, then publish it to the project issue tracker. Apply the `ready-for-agent` triage label - no need for additional triage.\\r\\n\\r\\n<spec-template>\\r\\n\\r\\n## Problem Statement\\r\\n\\r\\nThe problem that the user is facing, from the user\'s perspective.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Solution\\r\\n\\r\\nThe solution to the problem, from the user\'s perspective.\\r\\n\\r\\n## User Stories\\r\\n\\r\\nA LONG, numbered list of user stories. Each user story should be in the format of:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. As an <actor>, I want a <feature>, so that <benefit>\\r\\n\\r\\n<user-story-example>\\r\\n1. As a mobile bank customer, I want to see balance on my accounts, so that I can make better informed decisions about my spending\\r\\n</user-story-example>\\r\\n\\r\\nThis list of user stories should be extremely extensive and cover all aspects of the feature.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Implementation Decisions\\r\\n\\r\\nA list of implementation decisions that were made. This can include:\\r\\n\\r\\n- The modules that will be built/modified\\r\\n- The interfaces of those modules that will be modified\\r\\n- Technical clarifications from the developer\\r\\n- Architectural decisions\\r\\n- Schema changes\\r\\n- API contracts\\r\\n- Specific interactions\\r\\n\\r\\nDo NOT include specific file paths or code snippets. They may end up being outdated very quickly.\\r\\n\\r\\nException: if a prototype produced a snippet that encodes a decision more precisely than prose can (state machine, reducer, schema, type shape), inline it within the relevant decision and note briefly that it came from a prototype. Include:\\r\\n\\r\\n- A description of what makes a good test (only test external behavior, not implementation details)\\r\\n- Which modules will be tested\\r\\n- Prior art for the tests (i.e. similar types of tests in the codebase)\\r\\n\\r\\n## Out of Scope\\r\\n\\r\\nA description of the things that are out of scope for this spec.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Further Notes\\r\\n\\r\\nAny further notes about the feature.\\r\\n\\r\\n</spec-template>\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n### skills\\\\claude\\\\to-tickets\\\\SKILL.md\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: to-tickets\\r\\ndescription: Break a plan, spec, or the current conversation into a set of tracer-bullet tickets, each declaring its blocking edges, published to the configured tracker (edges as text in one file per ticket locally, or native blocking links on a real tracker).\\r\\ndisable-model-invocation: true\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# To Tickets\\r\\n\\r\\nBreak a plan, spec, or conversation into a set of **tickets**: tracer-bullet vertical slices, each declaring the tickets that **block** it.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe issue tracker and triage label vocabulary should have been provided to you. If not, tell the user to run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills`.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Process\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1. Gather context\\r\\n\\r\\nWork from whatever is already in the conversation context. If the user passes a reference (a spec path, an issue number or URL) as an argument, fetch it and read its full body and comments.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2. Explore the codebase (optional)\\r\\n\\r\\nIf you have not already explored the codebase, do so to understand the current state of the code. Ticket titles and descriptions should use the project\'s domain glossary vocabulary, and respect ADRs in the area you\'re touching.\\r\\n\\r\\nLook for opportunities to prefactor the code to make the implementation easier. \\"Make the change easy, then make the easy change.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n### 3. Draft vertical slices\\r\\n\\r\\nBreak the work into **tracer bullet** tickets.\\r\\n\\r\\n<vertical-slice-rules>\\r\\n\\r\\n- Each slice cuts a narrow but COMPLETE path through every layer (schema, API, UI, tests): vertical, NOT a horizontal slice of one layer\\r\\n- A completed slice is demoable or verifiable on its own\\r\\n- Each slice is sized to fit in a single fresh context window\\r\\n- Any prefactoring should be done first\\r\\n\\r\\n</vertical-slice-rules>\\r\\n\\r\\nGive each ticket its **blocking edges**: the other tickets that must complete before it can start. A ticket with no blockers can start immediately.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Wide refactors are the exception to vertical slicing.** A **wide refactor** is one mechanical change (rename a column, retype a shared symbol) whose **blast radius** fans across the whole codebase, so a single edit breaks thousands of call sites at once and no vertical slice can land green. Don\'t force it into a tracer bullet; sequence it as **expand–contract**. First expand: add the new form beside the old so nothing breaks. Then migrate the call sites over in batches sized by blast radius (per package, per directory), each batch its own ticket blocked by the expand, keeping CI green batch to batch because the old form still exists. Finally contract: delete the old form once no caller remains, in a ticket blocked by every migrate batch. When even the batches can\'t stay green alone, keep the sequence but let them share an integration branch that all block a final integrate-and-verify ticket; green is promised only there.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 4. Quiz the user\\r\\n\\r\\nPresent the proposed breakdown as a numbered list. For each ticket, show:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Title**: short descriptive name\\r\\n- **Blocked by**: which other tickets (if any) must complete first\\r\\n- **What it delivers**: the end-to-end behaviour this ticket makes work\\r\\n\\r\\nAsk the user:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Does the granularity feel right? (too coarse / too fine)\\r\\n- Are the blocking edges correct: does each ticket only depend on tickets that genuinely gate it?\\r\\n- Should any tickets be merged or split further?\\r\\n\\r\\nIterate until the user approves the breakdown.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 5. Publish the tickets to the configured tracker\\r\\n\\r\\nPublish the approved tickets. **How** depends on the tracker `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` configured; the tickets are the same either way, only the shape of the blocking edges changes:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Local files** → write one file per ticket under `.scratch/<feature-slug>/issues/<NN>-<slug>.md`, numbered from `01` in dependency order (blockers first). Each file\'s \\"Blocked by\\" lists the numbers/titles it depends on. Use the per-ticket file template below: one ticket per file, never a single combined file.\\r\\n- **A real issue tracker (GitHub, Linear, …)** → publish one issue per ticket in dependency order (blockers first) so each ticket\'s blocking edges can reference real identifiers. Use the platform\'s native blocking relationship where it has one; otherwise set each ticket\'s \\"Blocked by\\" to the blocking issues. If the source was an existing issue, make each ticket its sub-issue (tracker doc\'s operation). Apply the `ready-for-agent` triage label unless instructed otherwise; the tickets are agent-grabbable by construction.\\r\\n\\r\\nWork the **frontier**: any ticket whose blockers are all done. For a purely linear chain that means top to bottom.\\r\\n\\r\\nDo NOT close or modify any parent issue.\\r\\n\\r\\n<local-ticket-template>\\r\\n\\r\\n# <NN>: <Ticket title>\\r\\n\\r\\n**What to build:** the end-to-end behaviour this ticket makes work, from the user\'s perspective, not a layer-by-layer implementation list.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Blocked by:** the numbers/titles of the tickets that gate this one, or \\"None (can start immediately)\\".\\r\\n\\r\\n**Status:** ready-for-agent\\r\\n\\r\\n- [ ] Acceptance criterion 1\\r\\n- [ ] Acceptance criterion 2\\r\\n\\r\\n</local-ticket-template>\\r\\n\\r\\n<issue-template>\\r\\n\\r\\n## Parent\\r\\n\\r\\nA reference to the parent issue on the tracker (if the source was an existing issue, otherwise omit this section).\\r\\n\\r\\n## What to build\\r\\n\\r\\nThe end-to-end behaviour this ticket makes work, from the user\'s perspective, not layer-by-layer implementation.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Acceptance criteria\\r\\n\\r\\n- [ ] Criterion 1\\r\\n- [ ] Criterion 2\\r\\n\\r\\n## Blocked by\\r\\n\\r\\n- A reference to each blocking ticket, or \\"None (can start immediately)\\". Omit this section when blockers were set as native edges.\\r\\n\\r\\n</issue-template>\\r\\n\\r\\nIn either form, avoid specific file paths or code snippets: they go stale fast.
